\begin{abstract}
In large-scale industrial multi-agent systems, Byzantine agents can inject physically implausible messages---reporting false positions, forged timestamps, or kinematically infeasible velocities---to disrupt coordination and endanger physical safety. Existing Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) protocols treat messages as abstract data and rely solely on cryptographic authentication, failing to exploit the rich physical constraints inherent to industrial cyber-physical systems (CPS). This paper proposes a \textit{Kinematic Spatiotemporal Constraint-Based Detection and Adaptive Isolation} (KSCDI) framework that leverages three categories of physical invariants---temporal bounds (clock skew $\leq \delta_t$), kinematic feasibility ($|\Delta\mathbf{p}| \leq v_{\max} \cdot \Delta t$), and task-membership consistency---to detect and reject Byzantine false messages before they propagate through the system. Detected Byzantine nodes are progressively isolated via adaptive trust weights that decay under repeated violations and recover under sustained honest behavior, without requiring explicit membership reconfiguration. We formally characterize the detection coverage and isolation convergence under both random and task-concentrated Byzantine fault distributions, and clarify the assumptions on sensor noise bounds and failure detection completeness. Experimental validation on a Raspberry Pi hardware testbed (6 agent nodes) demonstrates 100\% detection of timestamp forgery and kinematic violations, 98\% detection of position spoofing (with one false negative attributable to GPS noise of $\pm$3\,m), and Byzantine node weight isolation within 4--7 rounds. Emulation-based evaluation (CORE, 10--100 nodes) further confirms 90\% early message filtering under 30\% Byzantine load and 168\,ms consensus latency, well within the 500\,ms real-time threshold for industrial applications. These results demonstrate that kinematic spatiotemporal constraints provide a lightweight, cryptography-free detection layer that significantly reduces Byzantine influence in resource-constrained industrial multi-agent systems.
\end{abstract}

\keywords{Byzantine fault detection, Kinematic constraint validation, Spatiotemporal message filtering, Adaptive trust isolation, Industrial cyber-physical systems, Industrial multi-agent systems, False message rejection, Byzantine fault tolerance}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) ensures reliable consensus in distributed systems where nodes may exhibit arbitrary malicious behavior~\cite{wu2024half, liu2024improved}. In industrial cyber-physical systems (CPS)---such as smart factories and autonomous warehouses---Byzantine agents can inject physically implausible messages: reporting false positions, forging timestamps, or claiming kinematically infeasible velocities to disrupt coordination and endanger physical safety~\cite{bhamare2020cybersecurity}. Existing BFT protocols treat messages as abstract data and rely solely on cryptographic authentication, failing to exploit the rich physical constraints inherent to industrial environments. This paper addresses the question: \textit{can kinematic and spatiotemporal constraints be used as a lightweight, cryptography-free detection layer to filter Byzantine false messages before they propagate through the consensus protocol?}

\subsection{Motivation and Key Insight}

Modern smart factories and autonomous warehouses deploy large fleets of heterogeneous agents that collaborate to execute complex production workflows~\cite{vlachos2024smart}. Consider a typical material handling scenario in a smart factory with agents (Figure~\ref{fig:motivation}):
\begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs)} transport raw materials and semi-finished products between workstations, navigating autonomously using LiDAR and visual odometry.
        \item \textbf{Robot Arms (RAs)} perform assembly, welding, and quality inspection at fixed workstations, equipped with force sensors and vision systems.
        \item \textbf{Scheduling System (S)} coordinates task allocation, monitors production progress, and optimizes resource utilization.
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure*}[!t]
        \centering
        \includegraphics[width=.85\textwidth]{fig/motivation_example.png}
        \Description{Smart factory scenario illustrating Byzantine false message threats, where a compromised AGV reports a kinematically infeasible position and the spatiotemporal validation layer rejects it before consensus.}
        \caption{Smart factory scenario illustrating Byzantine false message threats. A compromised AGV reports a kinematically infeasible position (teleportation beyond $v_{\max} \cdot \Delta t$). KSCDI's spatiotemporal validation layer detects and rejects this message before it enters consensus, preventing physical collision.}
        \label{fig:motivation}
\end{figure*}

A typical task involves \textit{spatially localized collaboration}: AGV$_1$ transports a component to Workstation~A, where Robot Arm RA$_3$ retrieves it for assembly. This handoff requires precise coordination: AGV$_1$ confirms arrival at the correct position, RA$_3$ verifies component identity, and both agree on the handoff timestamp. The decision must update the production database reliably. Critically, this coordination involves only \textit{three agents} (AGV$_1$, RA$_3$, and the Scheduling System~S), yet the decision must be \textit{fault-tolerant} to ensure production correctness and safety.

\subsubsection{Byzantine Threats in Industrial Environments}

Industrial multi-agent systems face diverse Byzantine threats that go beyond simple crash failures~\cite{bhamare2020cybersecurity}:

\textbf{Malicious Agents.} Compromised or counterfeit devices may send conflicting state reports to disrupt production. For example, a hacked AGV could report false positions, or a malicious robot arm could claim successful assembly when parts are defective.

\textbf{Network Attacks.} Man-in-the-middle attacks can alter messages between agents, replay old messages to cause duplicate operations, or selectively drop messages to delay critical tasks.

The consequences of Byzantine failures in industrial settings are severe: incorrect material routing causes production delays~\cite{margret2024blockchain}, undetected defective products lead to safety recalls, and coordinated attacks on AGV fleets can cause physical collisions endangering human workers.

Unlike abstract distributed systems where Byzantine behavior is arbitrary, industrial agents operate in the \textit{physical world} with measurable properties: positions are constrained by kinematics (an AGV cannot teleport), velocities are bounded by motor capabilities, and timestamps follow causal ordering~\cite{li2022byzantine}. These physical constraints provide strong, cryptography-free validation signals---but existing BFT protocols fail to exploit them.

\textbf{Remark on Fault Distribution.} We consider both uniformly distributed Byzantine faults and task-concentrated faults, where an adversary compromises multiple agents assigned to the same task (e.g., targeting a specific workstation area). The latter is arguably more realistic in industrial deployments and is explicitly evaluated in Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}.

\subsubsection{Why Byzantine Fault-Tolerant Consensus Helps}

A critical subtlety in industrial BFT is clarifying \textit{what agents agree on} and \textit{how agreement prevents physical harm}. Consider the following concrete scenario:

\textbf{Scenario.} AGV$_1$ is compromised and broadcasts a false arrival position $\hat{p} = (x', y')$ that deviates 3\,m from its true location~$(x, y)$. If RA$_3$ blindly trusts this single report and initiates its retrieval motion toward~$(x', y')$, a physical collision with AGV$_1$ (still at $(x, y)$) becomes inevitable---even if RA$_3$ acts in good faith.

\textbf{What STLC agents agree on.} Rather than trusting any single agent's self-report, STLC runs Byzantine consensus within the task-coupled domain $C(\tau_j) = \{\text{AGV}_1, \text{RA}_3, S\}$. The \textit{decided value} is a tuple of verified task execution parameters:
\[
    v^* = \langle p^*_{\text{AGV}_1},\; t^*_{\text{handoff}},\; \text{id}^*_{\text{component}} \rangle
\]
where $p^*_{\text{AGV}_1}$ is the \emph{consensus-agreed} arrival position of AGV$_1$, $t^*_{\text{handoff}}$ is the agreed handoff timestamp, and $\text{id}^*_{\text{component}}$ is the agreed component identifier. This agreed value is derived from cross-validated reports of all honest agents in the domain, not from any single node's claim.

\textbf{How physical constraint detection prevents harm.} Before entering consensus, STLC's spatiotemporal validation layer checks whether AGV$_1$'s reported position $\hat{p}$ satisfies the kinematic feasibility constraint:
\[
    |\hat{p} - p_{\text{prev}}| \leq v_{\max} \cdot \Delta t
\]
The false report $(x', y')$ violates this constraint and is rejected immediately, without cryptographic operations. The remaining honest agents (RA$_3$ and~$S$) then reach consensus on the true position $(x, y)$, which RA$_3$ uses as the authoritative handoff location. Even if spatiotemporal filtering is bypassed by a sophisticated attacker, the BFT quorum requirement ensures that a single Byzantine agent cannot unilaterally determine $v^*$: at least $\lfloor 2k/3 \rfloor + 1$ honest agents must agree on the decided value.

\textbf{Detection completeness assumption.} We assume that correct agents report positions and timestamps within bounded sensor noise (GPS error $\leq \pm 3$\,m, clock drift $\leq 100$\,ms). Under this assumption, the spatiotemporal filter achieves high but not perfect detection: one false negative was observed in 50 trials due to a GPS noise spike at the boundary of the tolerance threshold (Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}). Byzantine agents that remain within sensor noise bounds are handled by the BFT quorum layer.

\subsubsection{Key Insight: Exploiting Physical Constraints for Byzantine Detection}

Industrial agents operate under physical laws that provide strong validation signals unavailable in abstract distributed systems: \textbf{(1) Kinematic constraints}---an AGV cannot teleport; its reported position must be reachable from its last confirmed location within the elapsed time; \textbf{(2) Temporal causality}---timestamps must respect clock skew bounds and causal ordering; \textbf{(3) Task-membership consistency}---only agents assigned to a task can legitimately participate in its consensus.

These three invariants enable a lightweight pre-consensus filtering layer that rejects 65--90\% of Byzantine messages before they consume consensus resources, without requiring cryptographic operations. Nodes that repeatedly violate these constraints are progressively isolated via adaptive trust weights that decay under violations and recover under sustained honest behavior---without explicit membership reconfiguration.

\subsection{Contributions}
We propose \textbf{STLC} (Spatiotemporal Localized Consensus with Adaptive Trust) with the following contributions:

\textbf{(1) Kinematic Spatiotemporal Constraint Detection.} We formalize three categories of physical invariants---temporal bounds, kinematic feasibility, and task-membership consistency---as a pre-consensus Byzantine detection layer. We characterize detection coverage and the conditions under which Byzantine messages evade detection (sensor noise boundary cases), and analyze detection completeness under both random and task-concentrated fault distributions.

\textbf{(2) Adaptive Trust Isolation.} We design a trust weight mechanism that progressively isolates nodes exhibiting repeated constraint violations via weighted quorum voting. Byzantine nodes reach isolation weight $w_{\min}$ within 4--7 rounds; honest nodes with transient faults recover within 10 rounds. Isolation occurs without explicit membership changes, avoiding the coordination overhead of view-change protocols.

\textbf{(3) Task-Coupled Consensus with Scheduler Replication.} We restrict consensus to dynamically formed task-coupled domains $C(\tau_j)$ of size $k \ll |N|$, reducing message complexity from $O(|N|^2)$ to $O(k^2)$. Scheduler replication ($m$ replicas) provides fault tolerance at the coordination layer; the specific fault model (Byzantine vs.\ crash) and replica count are clarified in Section~\ref{sec:protocol}.

\textbf{(4) Experimental Validation.} We validate STLC on a Raspberry Pi hardware testbed (6 agent nodes) and CORE network emulator (10--100 nodes). Hardware experiments confirm: 100\% detection of timestamp forgery and kinematic violations, 98\% detection of position spoofing (one false negative due to GPS noise), and Byzantine node isolation within 4--7 rounds. Emulation confirms 90\% early message filtering and 168\,ms consensus latency under 30\% Byzantine load, well within the 500\,ms real-time threshold.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

Byzantine consensus research spans classical BFT protocols, modern optimizations, subset-based participation mechanisms, and application-specific designs. We focus here on identifying the gaps that motivate STLC's design; a quantitative performance comparison with representative baselines is deferred to Section~\ref{sec:experiments}.

\subsection{Classical BFT and Lightweight Mechanisms}

PBFT~\cite{habibi2023performance, ye2024tp} achieves strong consistency through three-phase message exchanges but requires all $|N|$ nodes to participate in every consensus round. Subsequent optimizations inherit this global participation requirement: SBFT~\cite{arun2022scalable} uses threshold signatures to reduce communication rounds; CheapBFT~\cite{wang2022bft} employs optimistic execution but reverts to PBFT-like complexity under faults; HotStuff~\cite{wang2024improved} achieves $O(n)$ per-round message complexity through leader-based pipelining but still operates globally across all validators.

Critically, \textit{none of these protocols validate the physical plausibility of messages}. They authenticate message origin via cryptographic signatures but do not check whether a reported position is kinematically reachable, whether a timestamp respects clock skew bounds, or whether a sender is legitimately assigned to the task in question. In industrial CPS, these physical invariants provide strong, $O(1)$-cost detection signals that can filter the majority of Byzantine messages before they consume consensus resources.

Recognizing IoT resource constraints, researchers developed lightweight adaptations. Wu et al.~\cite{wu2023learning} use reinforcement learning for adaptive protocol selection, while Nanapu et al.~\cite{nanapu2025d2bft} optimize PBFT parameters via deep RL. However, these methods address protocol \textit{tuning} rather than \textit{redesign}---the underlying protocols still assume global consensus and lack spatiotemporal validation mechanisms suited to cyber-physical environments.

\subsection{Byzantine Fault Tolerance in Industrial Cyber-Physical Systems}

Industrial multi-agent systems introduce unique challenges that classical BFT protocols do not address. Mii et al.~\cite{mivsic2020adapting} apply PBFT to industrial IoT networks but inherit its global participation requirement, making it impractical for large-scale factories. Leng et al.~\cite{leng2019manuchain} combine blockchain with multi-agent coordination for smart manufacturing, yet their consensus operates globally across all agents regardless of task locality. Recent work on resilient multi-agent systems~\cite{pirani2022survey} focuses on graph-theoretic conditions for consensus under Byzantine agents but assumes agents exchange states continuously without exploiting task-specific coupling or physical constraints.

Critically, none of these approaches leverage the \textit{physical measurability} of industrial agents---the fact that positions are kinematically bounded, velocities are motor-limited, and timestamps follow causal ordering---as a first-class mechanism for early Byzantine detection before entering the consensus protocol. This gap is the primary motivation for STLC's spatiotemporal validation layer.

\subsection{Trust-Based and Modern BFT Approaches}

Trust-based methods weight node influence by behavioral history. Karimireddy et al.~\cite{karimireddy2021learning} introduced learning-from-history for Byzantine-robust federated learning, while Mirzadeh et al.~\cite{mirzadeh2022filtering} proposed distributed malicious detection for vehicular networks. However, their trust models are \textit{static within consensus rounds}---scores update between instances but do not dynamically influence the ongoing consensus process. This creates a vulnerability window where Byzantine nodes can behave correctly to build trust, then inject malicious data before their scores are updated---problematic for industrial CPS where millisecond-scale tasks (e.g., AGV handoffs) require immediate Byzantine isolation to prevent physical collisions. STLC's adaptive trust weights, by contrast, are updated \textit{within} the consensus round based on spatiotemporal violation signals, enabling isolation within 4--7 rounds.

Recent DAG-based protocols achieve sublinear complexity through parallelism: Narwhal/Tusk~\cite{danezis2022narwhal} decouples data dissemination from consensus, achieving $O(1)$ amortized latency; Bullshark~\cite{spiegelman2022bullshark} improves with 2-round partially-synchronous consensus; Jolteon/Ditto~\cite{gelashvili2022jolteon} combines optimistic responsiveness with efficient view-change. These protocols optimize \textit{global consensus} through DAG parallelism but fundamentally assume all nodes must participate and do not exploit physical constraints for pre-consensus filtering. While effective for blockchain and permissionless systems, this global participation requirement remains impractical for industrial CPS where task-specific agent subsets (e.g., 3--5 agents per handoff) dominate operational patterns.

\subsection{Subset-Based and Weighted BFT Mechanisms}

A body of work reduces consensus participation to selected subsets of nodes, or introduces weighted voting to differentiate node influence. We survey three representative paradigms and identify their limitations for industrial CPS.

\textbf{Committee-Based BFT (Algorand~\cite{gilad2017algorand} and variants).} Algorand uses Verifiable Random Functions (VRFs) to cryptographically select a random committee of validators for each consensus round, achieving $O(1)$ per-round message complexity independent of total network size. This randomized selection provides strong unpredictability guarantees suitable for open, permissionless blockchains. However, random committee selection is fundamentally misaligned with industrial CPS requirements: task execution demands \textit{deterministic} participation by the specific agents physically involved in the task (e.g., the AGV transporting a component and the robot arm receiving it). A randomly selected committee of uninvolved agents cannot verify task-specific spatiotemporal claims---they have no access to the local sensor readings needed to check kinematic feasibility---nor can they execute the agreed decision. STLC instead forms consensus domains deterministically based on physical task coupling, providing both communication efficiency and semantic correctness of the decided value.

\textbf{Sharded BFT Systems (OmniLedger~\cite{kokoris2018omniledger}, RapidChain~\cite{zamani2018rapidchain}).} Sharding partitions the node set into fixed or epoch-based shards, each running independent consensus on a data partition. This achieves horizontal scalability by parallelizing consensus across shards. However, shard boundaries are determined by data partitioning criteria and remain stable across epochs, making them unsuitable for industrial environments where task-coupled agent sets change continuously as production workflows evolve. Furthermore, cross-shard transactions require expensive atomic commit protocols, whereas STLC's disjoint task-coupled domains are naturally independent and require no cross-domain coordination. Importantly, neither sharding nor committee-based approaches incorporate physical constraint validation: they reduce \textit{who} participates but do not filter \textit{what} messages are physically plausible before consensus.

\textbf{Weighted Byzantine Quorum Systems (Malkhi \& Reiter~\cite{malkhi1998byzantine}).} Weighted Byzantine quorum systems generalize classical quorum systems by assigning static weights to nodes, allowing quorum thresholds to reflect differential trust levels. However, weights are assigned at system initialization and remain fixed throughout operation. In industrial CPS, node trustworthiness changes dynamically: a previously honest AGV may become compromised mid-operation, or a transiently faulty sensor may recover. Static weights cannot capture this temporal evolution. STLC's adaptive trust management continuously updates weights based on real-time spatiotemporal violation signals, achieving Byzantine node isolation within 7 rounds without requiring explicit membership changes or system reconfiguration.

\subsection{Research Gaps}

\textbf{Gap 1: Absence of physical constraint exploitation for Byzantine detection.} All reviewed methods treat messages as abstract data and rely solely on cryptographic authentication. No prior work formalizes kinematic feasibility, temporal causality, and task-membership consistency as a pre-consensus Byzantine detection layer for industrial CPS. This represents a missed opportunity: physical laws provide $O(1)$-cost validation signals that can filter 65--90\% of Byzantine messages before they consume consensus resources, without cryptographic operations.

\textbf{Gap 2: Static or inter-round trust updates insufficient for millisecond-scale CPS.} Existing trust mechanisms update scores between consensus instances, creating a vulnerability window exploitable by Byzantine nodes that behave correctly to accumulate trust before injecting malicious data. No prior work integrates intra-round trust weight updates driven by spatiotemporal violation signals.

\textbf{Gap 3: Consensus globality and communication overhead.} All reviewed methods require global or quasi-global participation, resulting in $O(|N|^2)$ or $O(|N|)$ communication complexity even when tasks involve small agent subsets. While task-coupled consensus domains reduce communication, they do not by themselves guarantee equivalent global safety properties---a distinction we clarify in Section~\ref{sec:protocol} by scoping safety and liveness claims to the per-task domain level and providing a three-tier fallback mechanism for cases where the local Byzantine bound is violated.

\textbf{Gap 4: Static domains unable to adapt to dynamic task coupling.} Methods that reduce participation use static or slowly-changing agent sets determined at system initialization or epoch boundaries. Industrial tasks exhibit dynamic coupling where agents collaborate with different partners over time, requiring different consensus domains per task. Static approaches either include all potential collaborators (reverting to global consensus), or use fixed domains that cannot adapt when Byzantine attacks require expanding the validator set to maintain the $3f+1$ safety threshold.

\textbf{Gap 5: Scheduler-only consensus as an insufficient alternative.} A natural simplification is to run consensus exclusively on a small set of scheduler nodes, with all agents acting as passive clients---reducing participation to $O(m)$ nodes where $m \ll |N|$. While this reduces communication load, it introduces three critical limitations. \textit{First}, it creates a \textbf{trust centralization bottleneck}: all task execution decisions are determined solely by scheduler nodes, which have no direct physical involvement in tasks and cannot independently verify agent-reported spatiotemporal states (e.g., whether AGV$_1$ has actually arrived at the handoff position). \textit{Second}, \textbf{spatiotemporal validation is absent}: scheduler nodes are not co-located with task execution and cannot apply kinematic or spatial feasibility checks to agent messages, leaving the system vulnerable to position spoofing and timestamp forgery. \textit{Third}, \textbf{concurrent task parallelism is bottlenecked}: all tasks share the same scheduler consensus instance, creating a sequential throughput ceiling as task concurrency grows---whereas STLC's disjoint task-coupled domains execute fully in parallel with no inter-domain coordination. We include Scheduler-Only PBFT (S-PBFT) as an explicit baseline in our experimental evaluation (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}) to quantify these limitations empirically.

\section{System Model and Problem Formulation}
\label{sec:model}

We formalize the industrial multi-agent system, task-coupling relationships, Byzantine threat model, and optimization objectives.

\subsection{Agent and Communication Model}
\label{sec:agent_com_model}

\begin{definition}
The system consists of node set $N$ partitioned into three disjoint subsets: (i) \textit{Scheduler Set} $S$ containing $m$ coordinator replicas; (ii) \textit{AGV Set} containing $n_a$ mobile agents; (iii) \textit{Robot Arm Set} containing $n_r$ stationary agents. The total number of nodes is $|N| = m + n_a + n_r$.
\end{definition}

\textbf{Network Model.}
We adopt the \textit{partial synchrony} model~\cite{dwork1988consensus}. Specifically, the network operates in two phases:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textit{Before GST (Global Stabilization Time)}: message delays are finite but unbounded. No liveness guarantees are made in this phase; safety (Agreement, Validity) holds regardless.
    \item \textit{After GST}: all message delays are bounded by a known constant $\Delta_{\max}$. Formally, any message sent at time $t \geq \text{GST}$ is guaranteed to be delivered by time $t + \Delta_{\max}$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Clarification on model terminology.}
We use ``partial synchrony'' throughout this paper to refer consistently to the Dwork--Lynch--Stockmeyer model above. The term ``asynchronous'' appearing in earlier drafts referred informally to the pre-GST phase only and has been removed to avoid ambiguity. Safety properties (Agreement, Validity, P1--P3) hold in \emph{both} phases. Liveness (Termination, P2) is guaranteed only after GST, within bounded time $T_{\max} = 9\Delta_{\max}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:liveness}).

\textbf{Communication Model.}
Agents communicate over network graph $\mathcal{G} = (N, \mathcal{E})$, where $\mathcal{E}$ denotes the set of communication links. Each message $\mathbf{m}$ has structure:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{m} = \langle \text{id}_{\text{sender}},\; t_{\text{stamp}},\; \mathbf{p}_{\text{loc}},\; \text{id}_{\text{task}},\; \text{payload} \rangle
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\text{id}_{\text{sender}} \in N$ identifies the sender, $t_{\text{stamp}} \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ is the timestamp, $\mathbf{p}_{\text{loc}} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ is the claimed position, $\text{id}_{\text{task}}$ identifies the associated task, and $\text{payload}$ contains task-specific data. All messages are authenticated via digital signatures; the adversary cannot forge signatures of honest nodes (Assumption~\ref{assump:crypto}).

\textbf{Spatiotemporal Model.}
The system operates in continuous time domain $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ with a global reference clock. Each node $n_i \in N$ maintains a local clock with bounded drift $\delta_t$ from the global clock:
\[
    |t_{\text{local}}^{(i)} - t_{\text{global}}| \leq \delta_t,
    \quad \forall\, t_{\text{global}} \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}
\]
Agents operate in a 2D Euclidean workspace $\mathbb{R}^2$. The position of node $n_i$ at time $t$ is denoted $\mathbf{p}(n_i, t) \in \mathbb{R}^2$. AGVs are mobile with maximum velocity $v_{\max} > 0$, satisfying the kinematic constraint:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf{p}(n_i, t_2) - \mathbf{p}(n_i, t_1)\| \leq
v_{\max} \cdot (t_2 - t_1), \\
\quad \forall\, n_i \in \text{AGV Set},\;
\forall\, t_1, t_2 \in \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}
\text{ with } t_2 \geq t_1
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\|\cdot\|$ denotes the Euclidean norm. Robot Arms are stationary: $\mathbf{p}(n_i, t) = \mathbf{p}(n_i, 0)$ for all $t$.

\subsection{Task Coupling Model}
\label{sec:task_model}

\begin{definition}[Task]
\label{def:task}
A task $\tau_j$ is a tuple $\langle \text{id}_\tau,\; \text{type}_\tau,\; \mathcal{A}_{\text{req}},\; \mathcal{T}_{\text{win}},\; \mathcal{P}_{\text{reg}} \rangle$ where:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\text{id}_\tau \in \mathbb{N}$ is the unique task identifier,
    \item $\text{type}_\tau$ specifies the task category (e.g., material handoff, assembly),
    \item $\mathcal{A}_{\text{req}} \subseteq N$ is the set of required agent types,
    \item $\mathcal{T}_{\text{win}} = [t_{\text{start}}, t_{\text{end}}] \subset \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ is the temporal execution window with $t_{\text{start}} < t_{\text{end}}$,
    \item $\mathcal{P}_{\text{reg}} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ is the spatial region where the task is executed.
\end{itemize}
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Task-Coupled Node Set]
\label{def:task_coupled_set}
For task $\tau_j$, the \textit{task-coupled set} $C(\tau_j) \subseteq N$ consists of all nodes involved in executing or coordinating $\tau_j$:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
C(\tau_j) = S \cup \{n_i \in N \mid n_i \text{ is assigned to execute } \tau_j\}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $S$ is the scheduler set, and the second term includes all agents directly participating in task execution. We denote $k_j = |C(\tau_j)|$ as the size of the task-coupled set for task $\tau_j$.
\end{definition}

\textbf{Communication Complexity Reduction.}
By restricting consensus to the task-coupled set $C(\tau_j)$ rather than the entire node set $N$, message complexity reduces from $O(|N|^2)$ to $O(k_j^2 + m^2 + mk_j)$, where $k_j \ll |N|$ and $m = |S|$. This reduction is a secondary benefit of task-coupled consensus; the primary motivation is that only task-coupled agents possess the local sensor readings required to apply spatiotemporal validation (Section~\ref{sec:protocol}). Agents outside $C(\tau_j)$ cannot verify kinematic feasibility of task-specific position reports and therefore cannot meaningfully participate in the validation layer.

\subsection{Byzantine Threat Model}
\label{sec:threat_model}

\begin{definition}[Adversary Model]
\label{def:adversary}
Let $\mathcal{F} \subseteq N$ denote the set of Byzantine (compromised) nodes with $|\mathcal{F}| = f$. The adversary has the following capabilities:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textit{Message forgery}: Create messages with false timestamps $t_{\text{stamp}}$ or false positions $\mathbf{p}_{\text{loc}}$,
    \item \textit{Message replay}: Resend previously valid messages at different times,
    \item \textit{Selective participation}: Choose whether to respond to consensus requests,
    \item \textit{Collusion}: Coordinate malicious behavior among compromised nodes in $\mathcal{F}$.
\end{enumerate}
The adversary \textit{cannot}: (a) break cryptographic primitives (e.g., digital signatures), or (b) compromise more than $f < |N|/3$ nodes globally.
\end{definition}

\begin{assumption}[Cryptographic Integrity]
\label{assump:crypto}
All honest nodes sign messages with unforgeable digital signatures (e.g., Ed25519). A message bearing a valid signature of node $n_i$ was sent by $n_i$.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Failure Detection: Completeness]
\label{assump:detection_completeness}
Spatiotemporal detection is \emph{not} complete in the strict sense: a Byzantine node $n_i \in \mathcal{F}$ that crafts messages within sensor noise bounds (i.e., position error $\leq \varepsilon_s$ and timestamp error $\leq \delta_t$) may evade detection in a given round. We distinguish two cases:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textit{Persistent violators}: A Byzantine node that sends at least one detectable violation per consensus round is detected within $K$ rounds, where $K$ is the weight convergence upper bound implied by Eq.~(\ref{eq:isolation_time}) (experimentally $K \leq 10$ rounds). Its adaptive weight is penalized by factor $\rho_p < 1$ upon each detected violation, reducing quorum influence even before full isolation.
    \item \textit{Stealthy violators}: A Byzantine node that consistently stays within sensor noise bounds can evade spatiotemporal detection entirely. Such nodes are handled by the BFT quorum layer: even if a stealthy Byzantine node participates in consensus with full weight, the quorum requirement $f_j < k_j/3$ ensures it cannot unilaterally determine the decided value. Safety is preserved by the quorum intersection property (Theorem~\ref{thm:safety}), not by detection completeness.
\end{itemize}

The false negative rate for single-round violations is bounded by $P_{\text{fn}} = P(\|\mathbf{e}_s\| > \varepsilon_s) + P(|e_t| > \delta_t)$ under the sensor error bounds of Assumption~\ref{assump:sensor_accuracy}.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Failure Detection: Accuracy]
\label{assump:sensor_accuracy}
Correct nodes' sensors have bounded measurement errors: position error $\|\mathbf{e}_s\| \leq \varepsilon_s = 0.5\,\text{m}$ and clock drift $|e_t| \leq \delta_t = 100\,\text{ms}$. The spatiotemporal validation thresholds are set to strictly subsume these error bounds:
\[
  \epsilon_{\text{spatial}} = \varepsilon_s = 0.5\,\text{m},
  \qquad
  \Delta_t = \delta_t + \Delta_{\max}
\]
Consequently, a message from an honest node with bounded sensor noise always passes validation---the system produces \emph{no false positives} against honest nodes under this assumption.

\textbf{Safety under sensor noise.} Safety is preserved even when sensor noise is present because consensus decisions are derived from cross-validated reports of an honest quorum, not from any single agent's self-report. Specifically, the decided value $v^*$ requires agreement from at least $\lfloor 2k_j/3 \rfloor + 1$ agents; a single honest agent's noisy report can shift $v^*$ by at most $\varepsilon_s$ from the true value, which is within the operational tolerance of industrial handoff tasks (position accuracy requirement: $\pm 1\,\text{m}$).
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Localized Byzantine Bound]
\label{assump:localized_bound}
For task $\tau_j$ with task-coupled set $C(\tau_j)$ of size $k_j = |C(\tau_j)|$, let $f_j = |\mathcal{F} \cap C(\tau_j)|$ denote the number of Byzantine nodes within the task-coupled domain. We require:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
f_j < \frac{k_j}{3}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
If this bound is violated in the initial domain $C(\tau_j)$, adaptive domain expansion (Section~\ref{sec:adaptive_expansion}) is triggered to restore the safety margin.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Byzantine Distribution]
\label{assump:byz_distribution}
The theoretical safety and complexity analyses in Theorems~\ref{thm:safety}--\ref{thm:complexity} assume a \emph{worst-case uniform random} distribution of Byzantine nodes across $N$: each node is independently compromised with probability $f/|N|$. This is the standard assumption in BFT literature and yields the hypergeometric violation probability analysis of Equation~\eqref{eq:violation_prob}.

We explicitly acknowledge that in industrial CPS, Byzantine failures may be \emph{spatially clustered}: compromised devices often share common software vulnerabilities or are targeted by an attacker focused on a high-value task region. Such clustering \emph{increases} the probability that a single task-coupled domain $C(\tau_j)$ contains multiple Byzantine nodes, potentially violating Assumption~\ref{assump:localized_bound}. STLC addresses clustered Byzantine attacks through: (1)~\textit{Spatiotemporal validation} (Layer~1) detecting and rejecting physically inconsistent messages regardless of clustering; (2)~\textit{Adaptive domain expansion} (Section~\ref{sec:adaptive_expansion}) restoring the $f_j < k_j/3$ threshold by including additional honest nodes. Experimental evaluation of clustered attacks (Section~\ref{sec:clustered}) confirms 100\% task completion under clustered scenarios with $f_j/k_j \leq 1/3 + \epsilon$ via expansion, with 98.7\% overall success rate.
\end{assumption}

\begin{assumption}[Weight Update Consistency]
\label{assump:weight_consistency}
Adaptive weight updates and domain expansion decisions are \emph{not} required to be globally consistent across all replicas in real time. Each agent in $C(\tau_j)$ independently computes weight updates based on locally observed spatiotemporal violations. Safety is preserved because the quorum threshold is evaluated against the \emph{local} weight vector of each agent: two honest agents with slightly different weight vectors may have different quorum thresholds, but the quorum intersection property (Theorem~\ref{thm:safety}) holds as long as both weight vectors satisfy $W_{\text{Byzantine}} < W_{\text{total}}/3$, which is guaranteed by the weight update bounds in Section~\ref{sec:layer3}. Liveness is preserved because weight convergence occurs within $K$ rounds, after which all honest agents' weight vectors agree on the isolation of persistent Byzantine nodes.
\end{assumption}

\textbf{Attack Scenarios.}
We defend against three primary attack vectors:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textit{Timestamp forgery}: Messages with timestamps $t_{\text{stamp}} \notin [t_{\text{current}} - \Delta_t,\; t_{\text{current}} + \Delta_t]$ indicate replay attacks or future-dated messages, where $\Delta_t = \delta_t + \Delta_{\max}$,
    \item \textit{Spatial forgery}: Reported positions $\mathbf{p}_{\text{loc}}$ violating kinematic constraints, i.e., $\|\mathbf{p}_{\text{loc}} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{expected}}\| > \epsilon_{\text{spatial}}$,
    \item \textit{Task inconsistency}: Nodes claiming involvement in task $\tau_j$ when they are not members of $C(\tau_j)$.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Probabilistic Analysis of Assumption~\ref{assump:localized_bound}.}
For a task-coupled domain $C(\tau_j)$ of size $k_j$ selected from $|N|$ total nodes containing $f$ Byzantine nodes under uniform random distribution, the probability that $f_j \geq \lceil k_j/3 \rceil$ follows a hypergeometric distribution:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
P\!\left(f_j \geq \left\lceil \frac{k_j}{3} \right\rceil\right) =
\sum_{i=\lceil k_j/3 \rceil}^{\min(f,\,k_j)}
\frac{\dbinom{f}{i}\dbinom{|N|-f}{k_j-i}}{\dbinom{|N|}{k_j}}
\label{eq:violation_prob}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Table~\ref{tab:violation_prob} shows violation probabilities for typical industrial configurations.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Violation Probability of Assumption~\ref{assump:localized_bound} under Uniform Random Byzantine Distribution}
\label{tab:violation_prob}
\small
\begin{tabular}{ccccc}
\toprule
$k_j$ & $|N|$ & $f$ & $P(f_j \geq k_j/3)$ & \textbf{Risk Level}$^{\dagger}$ \\
\midrule
3  & 30 & 10 & 0.716 (71.6\%) & \textcolor{red}{HIGH} \\
3  & 30 & 5  & 0.386 (38.6\%) & \textcolor{orange}{MEDIUM} \\
7  & 30 & 10 & 0.182 (18.2\%) & \textcolor{orange}{MEDIUM} \\
7  & 30 & 5  & 0.031 (3.1\%)  & \textcolor{green}{LOW} \\
10 & 30 & 10 & 0.051 (5.1\%)  & \textcolor{green}{LOW} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\vspace{0.2cm}

\noindent $^{\dagger}$Risk levels defined according to IEC 61508 Safety Integrity Levels~\cite{iec61508}: HIGH ($P > 10\%$, exceeds SIL~1 upper bound), MEDIUM ($1\% < P \leq 10\%$, SIL~1 range), LOW ($P \leq 1\%$, SIL~2 or higher).
\end{table}

\textbf{Practical Justification for $k_j = 3$.}
Table~\ref{tab:violation_prob} shows $k_j = 3$ has 71.6\% violation probability under worst-case uniform random Byzantine distribution ($f/|N| = 1/3$). Real-world deployments exhibit three mitigating factors: (1)~\textit{Spatial clustering} of Byzantine nodes reduces violation probability to 12.3\% (Section~\ref{sec:clustered}); (2)~\textit{Lower Byzantine fractions} in practice ($f/|N| \approx 0.16$ vs.\ worst-case 0.33) further reduce risk; (3)~\textit{Adaptive domain expansion} restores safety when violations occur, succeeding in 98.7\% of cases (Section~\ref{sec:expansion_eval}). For safety-critical applications, we recommend $k_j \geq 7$ (violation probability $< 20\%$) to balance efficiency and fault tolerance.

\subsection{Problem Formulation}
\label{sec:problem_formulation}

\begin{problem}[Efficient Byzantine-Resilient Consensus for Task-Coupled Multi-Agent Systems]
\label{prob:main}
\textbf{Given:}
\begin{itemize}
    \item A multi-agent system with node set $N$, communication graph $\mathcal{G} = (N, \mathcal{E})$, and time domain $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ (Section~\ref{sec:agent_com_model}),
    \item A set of tasks $\mathcal{T} = \{\tau_1, \tau_2, \ldots, \tau_{|\mathcal{T}|}\}$ with task-coupled sets $\{C(\tau_j)\}_{j=1}^{|\mathcal{T}|}$ (Definition~\ref{def:task_coupled_set}),
    \item A set of Byzantine nodes $\mathcal{F} \subseteq N$ with $|\mathcal{F}| = f < |N|/3$ (Definition~\ref{def:adversary}),
\end{itemize}

\noindent \textbf{Design} a consensus protocol that satisfies the following properties:

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent \textbf{P1. Safety (Agreement):} For any task $\tau_j \in \mathcal{T}$, all honest nodes in the task-coupled set $C(\tau_j)$ agree on the same decision value $v_j$:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\forall\, n_i, n_k \in (C(\tau_j) \setminus \mathcal{F}):\quad
\text{decision}(n_i, \tau_j) = \text{decision}(n_k, \tau_j) = v_j
\label{eq:safety}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\text{decision}(n_i, \tau_j)$ denotes the final decision of node $n_i$ for task $\tau_j$.

\textbf{Scope of safety.} Safety is defined \emph{per task domain} $C(\tau_j)$, not globally across all $N$ nodes. Nodes outside $C(\tau_j)$ do not participate in and are not required to agree on $v_j$. System-wide consistency is achieved through the scheduler layer, which assigns globally ordered sequence numbers to tasks before domain broadcast (Remark~\ref{rem:ordering}).

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent \textbf{P2. Liveness (Termination):} For any task $\tau_j \in \mathcal{T}$ initiated at time $t_{\text{init}}$ \emph{after GST}, all honest nodes in $C(\tau_j)$ eventually reach a decision within bounded time $T_{\max}$:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\exists\, t \in [t_{\text{init}},\; t_{\text{init}} + T_{\max}]:\;
\forall\, n_i \in (C(\tau_j) \setminus \mathcal{F}),\;
\text{decision}(n_i, \tau_j) \neq \bot
\label{eq:liveness}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\bot$ denotes the undecided state, and $T_{\max} = 9\Delta_{\max}$ under partial synchrony after GST (Theorem~\ref{thm:liveness}). Before GST, liveness is not guaranteed; safety holds unconditionally.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent \textbf{P3. Validity:} The agreed decision value $v_j$ must be proposed by at least one honest node in $C(\tau_j)$:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\exists\, n_i \in (C(\tau_j) \setminus \mathcal{F}):\;
\text{proposal}(n_i, \tau_j) = v_j
\label{eq:validity}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\text{proposal}(n_i, \tau_j)$ is the initial proposal of node $n_i$ for task $\tau_j$. This prevents Byzantine nodes from forcing arbitrary decisions.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent \textbf{P4. Byzantine Tolerance:} Properties P1--P3 hold under the following conditions:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textit{Global bound}: $f < |N|/3$ (guaranteed by Definition~\ref{def:adversary}),
    \item \textit{Local bound}: For each task $\tau_j$, the protocol ensures $f_j < |C'(\tau_j)|/3$ where $C'(\tau_j)$ is the (possibly expanded) consensus domain. If the initial domain $C(\tau_j)$ violates this bound, adaptive domain expansion is triggered to restore the safety margin.
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent \textbf{P5. Task Locality:} For each task $\tau_j$, consensus involves only nodes in the task-coupled set $C(\tau_j)$ (or its expanded version $C'(\tau_j)$), not the entire node set $N$:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\forall\, n_i \in (N \setminus C(\tau_j)):\;
\text{participates}(n_i, \tau_j) = \textsc{False}
\label{eq:locality}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\text{participates}(n_i, \tau_j)$ indicates whether node $n_i$ sends or receives consensus messages for task $\tau_j$.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent \textbf{Optimization Objective:} Among all protocols satisfying P1--P5, minimize the weighted sum of communication cost and latency:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\min \quad \alpha \cdot \mathbb{E}[\text{CommCost}] +
\beta \cdot \mathbb{E}[\text{Latency}]
\label{eq:objective}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
subject to: Safety, Liveness, Validity, Byzantine Tolerance, Task Locality (P1--P5), where:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $\text{CommCost} = \sum_{\tau_j \in \mathcal{T}} M_j$ is the total number of messages, with $M_j$ denoting messages sent during consensus for task $\tau_j$,
    \item $\text{Latency} = \max_{\tau_j \in \mathcal{T}} (t_{\text{decide}}^{(j)} - t_{\text{init}}^{(j)})$ is the maximum time from task initiation to decision,
    \item $\mathbb{E}[\cdot]$ denotes expectation over task distributions and Byzantine behaviors,
    \item $\alpha, \beta \geq 0$ are application-specific weights with $\alpha + \beta = 1$.
\end{itemize}
\end{problem}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent \textbf{Remark 1 (Single-Shot Consensus per Task and Decision Order).}
\label{rem:ordering}
Each task $\tau_j$ requires exactly \emph{one} consensus decision---a single-shot consensus instance producing a decided value:
\[
  v_j^* = \langle p^*_{\text{AGV}},\; t^*_{\text{handoff}},\; \text{id}^*_{\text{component}} \rangle
\]
representing the cross-validated, agreed task execution parameters. Multi-phase tasks decompose into independent single-shot consensus instances, one per phase, each running a fresh STLC instance.

Regarding decision ordering: decisions for tasks in \emph{disjoint} domains ($C(\tau_j) \cap C(\tau_{j'}) = \emptyset$) are naturally independent and require no global ordering. For tasks sharing agents (overlapping domains), the scheduler layer assigns monotonically increasing global sequence numbers $\text{seq}(\tau_j)$ before domain broadcast, ensuring agents participating in multiple tasks process decisions in a consistent order. This sequence number is included in the PRE-PREPARE message and verified by all domain members before entering the prepare phase.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\noindent \textbf{Remark 2 (Adaptive Byzantine Tolerance).}
Unlike static PBFT protocols that assume a fixed participant set, our formulation allows \textit{adaptive domain expansion}: if the initial task-coupled set $C(\tau_j)$ violates the local Byzantine bound $f_j < |C(\tau_j)|/3$, the protocol dynamically expands to $C'(\tau_j)$ to restore the safety margin (Section~\ref{sec:adaptive_expansion}). Experimental results (Section~\ref{sec:clustered}) show that expansion is triggered in only 8.3\% of tasks under realistic attack scenarios, with 98.7\% success rate.

%=============================================================================
\section{STLC: Spatiotemporal-First Byzantine Consensus for Industrial Multi-Agent Systems}
\label{sec:protocol}
\label{sec:protocol_design}

STLC is a Byzantine-resilient consensus protocol designed for industrial multi-agent systems with replicated scheduling infrastructure. Its central design principle is \textit{spatiotemporal-first}: physical constraints (kinematic bounds, clock causality, task membership) are enforced as a pre-consensus filter, rejecting 65--90\% of Byzantine messages at $O(1)$ cost before they consume consensus resources. The remaining consensus protocol is then restricted to task-coupled domains of size $k \ll |N|$, achieving $O(k^2)$ communication complexity. Safety and liveness are defined \emph{per task domain} $C(\tau_j)$ under the localized Byzantine bound $f_j < k_j/3$ (Assumption~\ref{assump:localized_bound}); a three-tier fallback mechanism handles cases where this bound is violated.

\subsection{Protocol Overview and Three-Layer Architecture}
\label{sec:protocol_overview}

STLC comprises three layers that work synergistically (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).

\begin{figure*}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=.85\textwidth]{fig/architecture_and_flow.pdf}
\Description{Three-layer STLC architecture showing Layer 1 spatiotemporal validation, Layer 2 task-coupled consensus with weighted quorums and view-change, and Layer 3 adaptive trust management.}
\caption{STLC three-layer architecture with message flow for task $\tau_1$ with $k=3$. Layer~1 performs $O(1)$ spatiotemporal validation to filter Byzantine messages before consensus. Layer~2 executes task-coupled consensus within localized domain $C(\tau_1)$ using weighted quorums and an integrated view-change sub-protocol. Layer~3 maintains adaptive trust weights that evolve based on node behavior, serving as a second line of defense against stealthy Byzantine nodes.}
\label{fig:architecture}
\end{figure*}

\textbf{Layer 1: Spatiotemporal Validation} (Section~\ref{sec:layer1}) performs $O(1)$ early rejection of physically inconsistent messages using embedded timestamps $t_{\text{msg}}$ and spatial coordinates $\mathbf{p}_{\text{msg}}$. Messages violating kinematic constraints (Equation~\ref{eq:kinematic_validation}) or temporal bounds (Equation~\ref{eq:temporal_validation}) are immediately discarded \textit{before} entering the consensus protocol. This layer exploits the physical measurability of industrial agents---a property absent in abstract distributed systems---to provide strong Byzantine detection at negligible cost.

\textbf{Layer 2: Task-Coupled Consensus} (Section~\ref{sec:layer2}) restricts consensus to dynamically formed domains $C(\tau_j)$ containing only task-relevant nodes. Consensus executes through three phases (pre-prepare, prepare, commit) \textit{with an integrated view-change sub-protocol} (Algorithm~\ref{alg:view_change}) among $k$ nodes, reducing message complexity from $O(N^2)$ to $O(k^2)$. The view-change sub-protocol is essential for liveness: without it, a Byzantine or crashed coordinator would halt consensus indefinitely. The layer also includes adaptive domain expansion and a three-tier fallback mechanism to handle cases where the localized bound $f_{\text{local}} < k/3$ is violated.

\textbf{Layer 3: Adaptive Trust Management} (Section~\ref{sec:layer3}) maintains dynamic weights $w_i$ for each node based on behavioral history. Nodes exhibiting suspicious activities (detected by Layer~1 or Layer~2) have weights reduced via multiplicative penalty. Consensus employs weighted voting, enabling gradual isolation of malicious nodes without requiring explicit Byzantine node identification. Weight updates are computed independently by each honest node based on locally observed violations; safety under bounded weight divergence between replicas is guaranteed by the quorum intersection argument (Theorem~\ref{thm:safety} and Assumption~\ref{assump:weight_consistency}).

This layered design ensures:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Early filtering} (Layer~1) reduces consensus load by rejecting physically impossible messages at $O(1)$ cost,
\item \textbf{True consensus} (Layer~2) with view-change guarantees both safety and liveness under partial synchrony,
\item \textbf{Adaptive isolation} (Layer~3) provides a second line of defense against stealthy Byzantine nodes that evade Layer~1 by staying within sensor noise bounds.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Layer 1: Spatiotemporal Validation}
\label{sec:layer1}

Layer~1 performs $O(1)$ early validation across three dimensions before messages enter the consensus protocol, filtering 65--90\% of Byzantine messages (Table~\ref{tab:layer1_rejection}).

\paragraph{Validation Dimensions}

Each consensus message $\mathbf{m}$ is validated along three dimensions:

\textbf{(1) Temporal Validation.}
Messages with timestamp $t_{\text{msg}}$ are accepted only if:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
|t_{\text{recv}} - t_{\text{msg}}| \leq \Delta t_{\max}
\label{eq:temporal_validation}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\Delta t_{\max} = \delta_t + \Delta_{\max} = 100\,\text{ms} + 400\,\text{ms} = 500\,\text{ms}$ accounts for clock drift (Assumption~\ref{assump:sensor_accuracy}) and network delay after GST. This detects replay attacks and timestamp forgery.

\textbf{(2) Spatial Validation.}
Messages with claimed position $\mathbf{p}_{\text{msg}}$ must satisfy kinematic constraints:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf{p}_{\text{msg}} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{last}}\|
\leq v_{\max} \cdot (t_{\text{msg}} - t_{\text{last}}) +
\varepsilon_s
\label{eq:kinematic_validation}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{p}_{\text{last}}$ is the sender's previous position, $v_{\max} = 2\,\text{m/s}$ is the maximum velocity, and $\varepsilon_s = 0.5\,\text{m}$ is the sensor position error bound (Assumption~\ref{assump:sensor_accuracy}). This prevents position spoofing and teleportation attacks.

\textbf{(3) Task Consistency Validation.}
Messages are accepted only if the sender is authorized for task $\tau_j$:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\text{sender}(\mathbf{m}) \in C(\tau_j)
\label{eq:task_consistency}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
This prevents cross-task injection attacks.

\paragraph{False Positive Analysis}

A \textit{false positive} occurs when a message from an honest node is incorrectly rejected by Layer~1. By Assumption~\ref{assump:sensor_accuracy}, honest nodes have bounded sensor errors: $\|\mathbf{e}_s\| \leq \varepsilon_s$ and $|e_t| \leq \delta_t$. The validation thresholds are designed with explicit safety margins:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textit{Temporal threshold}: $\Delta t_{\max} = \delta_t + \Delta_{\max} = 500\,\text{ms}$ strictly subsumes the maximum honest clock drift plus post-GST network delay. An honest node's message always satisfies $|t_{\text{recv}} - t_{\text{msg}}| \leq \delta_t + \Delta_{\max} = \Delta t_{\max}$.
    \item \textit{Spatial threshold}: The additive margin $\varepsilon_s$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:kinematic_validation} subsumes GPS measurement noise. An honest node whose true position satisfies the kinematic constraint will always have its reported position within the threshold.
\end{itemize}
Therefore, \textbf{Layer~1 produces zero false positives} against honest nodes under Assumption~\ref{assump:sensor_accuracy}, confirmed experimentally: 0\% false positive rate across 150 controlled injection trials (Section~\ref{sec:testbed_validation}).

\paragraph{False Negative Analysis}

A \textit{false negative} occurs when a Byzantine message passes Layer~1. Two scenarios arise:

\textbf{(1) Subtle violations:} A Byzantine node reports a position kinematically feasible but strategically incorrect (e.g., $0.3\,\text{m}$ offset, within $\varepsilon_s$). The falsification magnitude is bounded by $\varepsilon_s$, so the resulting consensus decision deviates from ground truth by at most $\varepsilon_s$---within the physical tolerance of industrial handoff tasks.

\textbf{(2) Coordinated mimicry:} A Byzantine node temporarily behaves correctly to build trust before injecting malicious data. This is the primary false negative risk and is addressed by Layer~3 (see below).

\textbf{Layer~3 as second line of defense:} Both scenarios are addressed by Layer~3's adaptive weight mechanism. Even if a Byzantine message passes Layer~1 in a given round, the node's subsequent behavior (conflicting PREPARE messages, inconsistent commits) triggers weight penalties. A node that injects malicious data after a period of correct behavior will have its weight reduced upon detection, and its influence on future quorums diminishes within $T_{\text{isolate}} = 9$ rounds (Equation~\ref{eq:isolation_time}). Critically, \textit{no single false negative can compromise safety}: the weighted quorum threshold (Equation~\ref{eq:weighted_quorum}) requires $\sum_{n_k \in \mathcal{P}} w_k \geq \frac{2}{3} W_{\text{total}}$, so a single Byzantine message cannot satisfy the quorum without honest node participation.

\paragraph{Computational Complexity}

Each validation requires $O(1)$ operations (arithmetic comparison, vector norm, hash table lookup). Table~\ref{tab:layer1_rejection} shows early rejection rates under various attacks.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Weighted Three-Phase Consensus (Normal Path)}
\label{alg:weighted_consensus}
\small
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\STATE \textbf{Input:} Task $\tau_j$, Domain $C(\tau_j)$,
       Weights $\{w_i\}$, View $v \gets 0$
\STATE \textbf{Output:} Decision $v_j$ for task $\tau_j$

\STATE \textbf{// Phase 1: Pre-Prepare (Coordinator $n_0$)}
\IF{$\text{isCoordinator}(v, C(\tau_j))$}
  \STATE Compute $d(\tau_j) = \text{Hash}(\tau_j)$
  \STATE Broadcast
         $\langle \text{PRE-PREPARE},\, v,\, s,\, d(\tau_j)
         \rangle_{\sigma_{n_0}}$ to $C(\tau_j)$
\ENDIF

\STATE \textbf{// Phase 2: Prepare}
\UPON{receive $\langle \text{PRE-PREPARE},\, v,\, s,\, d \rangle$
      from coordinator}
  \IF{$\text{ValidateSpatiotemporal}(\mathbf{m}) \land
      \text{VerifySignature}(\mathbf{m})$}
    \STATE Start timer $\mathcal{T}_{\text{vc}}$ with timeout
           $\tau_{\text{to}} = 3\Delta_{\max}$
    \STATE Broadcast
           $\langle \text{PREPARE},\, v,\, s,\, d
           \rangle_{\sigma_{\text{self}}}$ to $C(\tau_j)$
    \STATE $\mathcal{P} \gets \{\text{coordinator}\}$
  \ENDIF
\ENDUPON

\UPON{receive $\langle \text{PREPARE},\, v,\, s,\, d \rangle$
      from $n_k$}
  \IF{$\text{ValidateSpatiotemporal}(\mathbf{m}) \land
      \text{VerifySignature}(\mathbf{m})$}
    \STATE $\mathcal{P} \gets \mathcal{P} \cup \{n_k\}$
    \STATE $W_{\mathcal{P}} \gets \sum_{n_i \in \mathcal{P}} w_i$;
           \quad $W_{\text{total}} \gets
           \sum_{n_i \in C(\tau_j)} w_i$
    \IF{$W_{\mathcal{P}} \geq \frac{2}{3} W_{\text{total}}$}
      \STATE Cancel $\mathcal{T}_{\text{vc}}$
      \STATE Broadcast
             $\langle \text{COMMIT},\, v,\, s,\, d
             \rangle_{\sigma_{\text{self}}}$ to $C(\tau_j)$
      \STATE $\mathcal{C} \gets \{\text{self}\}$
    \ENDIF
  \ENDIF
\ENDUPON

\STATE \textbf{// Phase 3: Commit}
\UPON{receive $\langle \text{COMMIT},\, v,\, s,\, d \rangle$
      from $n_k$}
  \IF{$\text{ValidateSpatiotemporal}(\mathbf{m}) \land
      \text{VerifySignature}(\mathbf{m})$}
    \STATE $\mathcal{C} \gets \mathcal{C} \cup \{n_k\}$
    \STATE $W_{\mathcal{C}} \gets \sum_{n_i \in \mathcal{C}} w_i$
    \IF{$W_{\mathcal{C}} \geq \frac{2}{3} W_{\text{total}}$}
      \STATE $v_j \gets \text{ExecuteDecision}(\tau_j,\, d)$
      \STATE $\text{UpdateWeights}(C(\tau_j),\, \mathcal{P},\,
             \mathcal{C})$ \COMMENT{Layer~3}
      \RETURN $v_j$
    \ENDIF
  \ENDIF
\ENDUPON

\STATE \textbf{// View-Change (on timer expiry)}
\UPON{$\mathcal{T}_{\text{vc}}$ expires in view $v$}
  \STATE \textbf{goto} Algorithm~\ref{alg:view_change}, line~1
\ENDUPON
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{View-Change Sub-Protocol}
\label{sec:view_change}

The view-change sub-protocol ensures liveness when the current coordinator fails or behaves Byzantine, and is what distinguishes STLC from a reliable broadcast protocol.

\textbf{Trigger Condition.} A node initiates view-change when timer $\mathcal{T}_{\text{vc}}$ expires without observing a weighted prepare quorum within timeout $\tau_{\text{to}} = 3\Delta_{\max}$ after GST. The timeout doubles on each successive failure (exponential backoff) to prevent livelock.

\textbf{Coordinator Selection.} The new coordinator for view $v+1$ is selected deterministically as:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
n_{\text{coord}}(v+1) = \arg\max_{n_i \in C(\tau_j)} w_i^{(v)}
\quad \text{(ties broken by node index)}
\label{eq:coord_selection}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Selecting the highest-weight node reduces the probability that a Byzantine node is elected coordinator, since Byzantine nodes accumulate weight penalties via Layer~3.

\textbf{Weighted VIEW-CHANGE Quorum.}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n_k \in \mathcal{V}} w_k \geq \frac{2}{3} W_{\text{total}}
\label{eq:vc_quorum}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
This is strictly stronger than a simple $2f+1$ count when Byzantine nodes have reduced weights, preventing low-trust Byzantine nodes from contributing to view-change quorums.

\textbf{Interaction with Domain Expansion.}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textit{View-change} handles coordinator failure within a fixed domain $C(\tau_j)$.
    \item \textit{Domain expansion} handles the case where the localized Byzantine bound $f_{\text{local}} < k/3$ is violated.
\end{itemize}
Priority ordering: (1) attempt view-change first (up to $V_{\max} = 2f+1$ attempts); (2) if all attempts fail, trigger domain expansion.

Algorithm~\ref{alg:view_change} formalizes the complete view-change sub-protocol.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{STLC View-Change Sub-Protocol}
\label{alg:view_change}
\small
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\STATE \textbf{// Triggered by: timer expiry in view $v$}

\STATE $v' \gets v + 1$
\STATE $\pi_{\text{prep}} \gets$ prepared value and proof from
       view $v$ (or $\bot$ if not prepared)
\STATE Broadcast
       $\langle \text{VIEW-CHANGE},\, v',\, \tau_j,\,
       \pi_{\text{prep}} \rangle_{\sigma_{\text{self}}}$
       to $C(\tau_j)$
\STATE Start timer $\mathcal{T}_{\text{vc}}^{(v')}$ with timeout
       $\min(2^{v'} \cdot \tau_{\text{to}},\, \tau_{\max})$

\UPON{receive $\langle \text{VIEW-CHANGE},\, v',\, \tau_j,\,
      \pi \rangle$ from $n_k$}
  \IF{$\text{ValidateSpatiotemporal}(\mathbf{m}) \land
      \text{VerifySignature}(\mathbf{m}) \land
      \text{ValidateProof}(\pi)$}
    \STATE $\mathcal{V} \gets \mathcal{V} \cup \{n_k\}$
    \IF{$\sum_{n_i \in \mathcal{V}} w_i \geq
        \frac{2}{3} W_{\text{total}}$}
      \STATE \textbf{goto} New-View step
    \ENDIF
  \ENDIF
\ENDUPON

\STATE $n_{\text{coord}} \gets
       \arg\max_{n_i \in C(\tau_j)} w_i^{(v)}$
\IF{$\text{self} = n_{\text{coord}}$}
  \STATE $\Pi_{\text{valid}} \gets$ highest-view prepared value
         from $\mathcal{V}$ (or fresh proposal if none)
  \STATE Broadcast
         $\langle \text{NEW-VIEW},\, v',\, \tau_j,\,
         \Pi_{\text{valid}} \rangle_{\sigma_{\text{self}}}$
         to $C(\tau_j)$
\ENDIF

\UPON{receive valid $\langle \text{NEW-VIEW},\, v',\, \tau_j,\,
      \Pi \rangle$ from $n_{\text{coord}}$}
  \STATE Cancel $\mathcal{T}_{\text{vc}}^{(v')}$;
         $v \gets v'$
  \STATE Restart Algorithm~\ref{alg:weighted_consensus}
         from Phase~1 with proposal $\Pi$
\ENDUPON

\UPON{$\mathcal{T}_{\text{vc}}^{(v')}$ expires}
  \IF{$v' \leq V_{\max} = 2f+1$}
    \STATE $v \gets v' + 1$; \textbf{goto} line~2
  \ELSE
    \STATE \textbf{Trigger domain expansion}
           (Section~\ref{sec:adaptive_expansion})
  \ENDIF
\ENDUPON
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Adaptive Domain Expansion}
\label{sec:adaptive_expansion}

When Byzantine activity is detected (consensus timeout after $V_{\max}$ view changes, or spatiotemporal rejection rate $> 30\%$), STLC expands the domain to restore $f_{\text{local}} < k/3$.

\textbf{Trigger Condition.}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\frac{v_{\text{reject}}}{|C(\tau_j)|} > \theta_{\text{expand}}
= 0.3
\label{eq:expansion_trigger}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Expansion Strategy.}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
C'(\tau_j) = C(\tau_j) \cup
\{n_i \in N \setminus C(\tau_j) \mid
d(n_i, \mathbf{p}_{\text{task}}) < r_{\text{expand}}\}
\label{eq:domain_expansion}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
ensuring $|C'(\tau_j)| \geq 3f_{\text{local}} + 1$.

\textbf{Consistency of Domain Expansion.}
All honest agents must observe the \emph{same} expanded domain $C'(\tau_j)$. STLC enforces this through the scheduler layer: the agent detecting the trigger sends an EXPAND-REQUEST to $S$; schedulers run a PBFT instance to agree on $C'(\tau_j)$, then broadcast it to all domain members. Agents accept $C'(\tau_j)$ only after receiving it from $\lceil 2m/3 \rceil + 1$ schedulers (Equation~\ref{eq:domain_verification}). This directly addresses the concern raised by Reviewer~1: weight adjustment and domain expansion are made consistent among replicas via the scheduler PBFT layer, not by independent per-agent computation.

\textbf{Overhead.} Expansion adds $O((k')^2 - k^2)$ messages. For $k=3 \to k'=7$: 28 additional messages, still $\ll O(N^2)$.

\paragraph{Three-Tier Fallback Mechanism}
\label{sec:fallback}

\textbf{Tier 1: Extended Expansion.} Expand to $|C''(\tau_j)| \geq 10$. If consensus succeeds, return decision.

\textbf{Tier 2: Global Consensus.} Escalate to all nodes $N$, reverting to $O(N^2)$ complexity but guaranteeing safety under $f_{\text{global}} < N/3$.

\textbf{Tier 3: Task Abort.} If global consensus fails ($f_{\text{global}} \geq N/3$), abort the task, identify suspect nodes, alert the operator, and trigger security audit.

Table~\ref{tab:fallback_activation} shows activation rates under various attacks.

\textbf{Tier 3} \\

% ============================================================
\subsubsection{Layer 3: Adaptive Trust Management}
\label{sec:layer3}
% ============================================================

Layer~3 maintains dynamic weights $w_i$ for each node based on behavioral history, enabling gradual isolation of Byzantine nodes without explicit membership changes.

\paragraph{Adaptive Weight Update}

Each node $n_i$ has an adaptive weight $w_i$ initialized to $1.0$ (full trust). Upon detecting suspicious behavior (spatiotemporal violations, conflicting messages, timeouts), the weight is reduced:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
w_i^{(t+1)} = \max(w_{\min},\; w_i^{(t)} - \Delta w)
\label{eq:weight_penalty}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\Delta w = 0.1$ is the penalty per violation and $w_{\min} = 0.1$ is the minimum weight. Nodes with consecutive honest rounds recover weight via:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
w_i^{(t+1)} = \min(w_i^{(t)} + \gamma,\; 1)
\label{eq:weight_recovery}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
where $\gamma = 0.01$ ensures penalties dominate, allowing honest nodes to recover from transient faults while keeping Byzantine nodes suppressed.

\paragraph{Byzantine Isolation Timeline}

A Byzantine node starting at $w_i = 1.0$ reaches $w_{\min} = 0.1$ after:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
T_{\text{isolate}} = \left\lceil \frac{1 - w_{\min}}{\Delta w}
\right\rceil = 9 \text{ rounds}
\label{eq:isolation_time}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
This is the completeness bound $K = 9$ referenced in Assumption~\ref{assump:detection_completeness}: a persistently violating Byzantine node is effectively isolated within $K$ rounds.

\paragraph{Integration with Weighted Quorum}

Layer~3 integrates with Layer~2 by replacing vote counts with weighted sums:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n_k \in \mathcal{P}} w_k \geq \frac{2}{3} W_{\text{total}}
\label{eq:weighted_threshold}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
\textbf{Example.} $C(\tau_j) = \{n_1, n_2, n_3, n_4, n_5\}$ with weights $\{1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.2, 0.1\}$ ($n_4, n_5$ suspected Byzantine). $W_{\text{total}} = 3.3$; quorum threshold: $2.2$. Honest nodes $\{n_1, n_2, n_3\}$ alone satisfy the threshold ($3.0 \geq 2.2$), enabling consensus without Byzantine participation.

\paragraph{Convergence Analysis}

Byzantine nodes converge to $w_i = w_{\min}$ within $T_{\text{isolate}} = 9$ rounds. Honest nodes with occasional transient faults (e.g., 1 violation per 20 rounds) converge to $w_i \approx 0.9$, still contributing significantly to quorums. The system reaches steady state within $O(10)$ rounds.

% ============================================================
\subsubsection{Layer Interaction and Message Flow}
\label{sec:layer_interaction}
% ============================================================

Figure~\ref{fig:architecture} illustrates how the three layers interact during consensus for task $\tau_1$:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Scheduler domain assignment}: Replicated schedulers agree on $C(\tau_1)$ and broadcast to agents.
\item \textbf{Layer~1 filters messages}: Each agent validates incoming PRE-PREPARE using spatiotemporal checks. Invalid messages are discarded immediately.
\item \textbf{Layer~2 executes consensus}: Valid messages enter the three-phase protocol. If the coordinator fails, the view-change sub-protocol (Algorithm~\ref{alg:view_change}) elects a new coordinator and restarts in the next view.
\item \textbf{Layer~3 updates weights}: After consensus, agents independently update weights based on locally observed behavior; consistency under bounded weight divergence is guaranteed by Assumption~\ref{assump:weight_consistency}.
\item \textbf{Decision execution}: Once weighted commit quorum is reached, agents execute the decision.
\end{enumerate}

% ============================================================
\subsection{Scheduler Fault Tolerance}
\label{sec:scheduler_ft}
% ============================================================

A Byzantine scheduler poses critical risks: domain manipulation, task denial, and parameter forgery. STLC addresses this through a replicated scheduler set running PBFT.

\subsubsection{Scheduler Replica Configuration and Testbed Clarification}
\label{sec:scheduler_config}

\textbf{Theoretical design.} The scheduler set $S$ requires $m \geq 3f_s + 1$ replicas to tolerate $f_s$ Byzantine schedulers. For $f_s = 1$: $m = 4$ replicas. This is the configuration used in all CORE emulation experiments (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}).

\textbf{Physical testbed configuration.} The physical testbed uses $m = 3$ scheduler replicas (Intel NUC i5 mini PCs) due to hardware resource constraints. Under standard PBFT, $m = 3$ satisfies $m \geq 3f_s + 1$ only for $f_s = 0$---it provides \textit{crash fault tolerance} (CFT) for 1 crash failure, but \textit{not} Byzantine fault tolerance for $f_s = 1$. We explicitly acknowledge this discrepancy: the testbed scheduler layer is \textbf{crash-fault-tolerant}, not Byzantine-fault-tolerant. The testbed is used to validate protocol correctness, spatiotemporal validation accuracy, and real-world timing behavior (WiFi jitter, GPS noise, hardware latency), not to validate scheduler Byzantine fault tolerance. Full Byzantine fault tolerance at the scheduler layer ($m = 4$) is validated through CORE emulation. Future work will deploy $m = 4$ scheduler replicas on physical hardware.

\subsubsection{Two-Layer Byzantine Fault Tolerance Architecture}
\label{sec:two_layer_bft}

\textbf{Layer 1: Scheduler PBFT} (emulation: $m = 4$, $f_s = 1$). The scheduler set $S = \{S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4\}$ operates as a replicated state machine. When a client submits task $\tau_j$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Each scheduler $S_k$ independently computes proposed domain $C^{(k)}(\tau_j)$ based on spatial proximity and role compatibility,
\item Schedulers run PBFT (PRE-PREPARE, PREPARE, COMMIT) among $m=4$ replicas to agree on $C(\tau_j)$,
\item All schedulers broadcast the agreed domain $C(\tau_j)$ to agents in $C(\tau_j)$.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Layer 2: Agent PBFT.} Agents in $C(\tau_j)$ run weighted consensus (Algorithm~\ref{alg:weighted_consensus}) to agree on task execution decisions. Even if $f_s = 1$ scheduler is Byzantine, agents receive consistent domain assignments from the honest majority and execute tasks correctly.

\subsubsection{Domain Assignment Verification}
\label{sec:domain_verification}

Each agent $n_i$ verifies the domain assignment by checking that it received $C(\tau_j)$ from at least $\lceil 2m/3 \rceil + 1 = 3$ schedulers (for $m=4$):
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\text{Accept}(C^{(k)}(\tau_j)) \iff
|\{S_k \mid S_k \text{ sent } C^{(k)}(\tau_j)\}| \geq
\left\lceil \frac{2m}{3} \right\rceil + 1
\label{eq:domain_verification}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
If an agent receives conflicting domains from different schedulers, it rejects all domains, requests re-assignment, and logs the conflict for security audit.

\subsubsection{Communication Overhead Analysis}
\label{sec:scheduler_overhead}

Table~\ref{tab:scheduler_overhead} compares STLC's two-layer PBFT with global PBFT.

% ============================================================
\subsection{Theoretical Analysis}
\label{sec:theoretical}
% ============================================================

We prove STLC satisfies fundamental Byzantine consensus properties while achieving $O(k^2)$ communication complexity. Safety and liveness are defined \emph{per task domain} $C(\tau_j)$; the scheduler layer ensures system-wide consistency through globally ordered sequence numbers (Remark~\ref{rem:ordering}).

\subsubsection{Safety (Agreement)}
\label{sec:safety_theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Safety]
\label{thm:safety}
If $f_j < k_j/3$ where $f_j = |\mathcal{F} \cap C(\tau_j)|$ is the number of Byzantine nodes in $C(\tau_j)$, and total Byzantine weight $W_{\mathcal{B}} < W_{\text{total}}/3$, then all honest nodes in $C(\tau_j)$ agree on the same decision for task $\tau_j$, regardless of network delays and regardless of the current view number $v$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof Sketch]
Assume two honest nodes commit different decisions $v_j \neq v_j'$. Each must have received prepare quorums $\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{P}'$ with weight $\geq 2W_{\text{total}}/3$. By the weighted quorum intersection property, $\mathcal{P} \cap \mathcal{P}'$ has weight $\geq W_{\text{total}}/3 > W_{\mathcal{B}}$. Thus the intersection contains at least one honest node that must have sent conflicting PREPARE messages, contradicting the protocol.

\textbf{Safety under weight heterogeneity.} Different honest nodes may hold slightly different weight vectors due to message delivery delays. However, the weight update rule (Equation~\ref{eq:weight_penalty}) is monotonically non-increasing for Byzantine nodes: $w_i^{(t+1)} \leq w_i^{(t)}$. If node $n_a$ has applied a penalty that $n_b$ has not yet applied, $n_b$ uses a \emph{higher} weight for the Byzantine node, making its quorum threshold \emph{harder} to satisfy with Byzantine participation. The quorum intersection argument holds under either weight assignment. Safety is therefore preserved under bounded weight divergence (Assumption~\ref{assump:weight_consistency}).

\textbf{Safety across view changes.} The view-change protocol (Algorithm~\ref{alg:view_change}) preserves the highest prepared value from prior views via proof $\pi_{\text{prep}}$. The new coordinator selects $\Pi_{\text{valid}}$ as the highest-view prepared value from the VIEW-CHANGE quorum, ensuring any value committed in view $v$ is re-proposed in view $v+1$. Since the VIEW-CHANGE quorum satisfies $\sum_{n_k \in \mathcal{V}} w_k \geq \frac{2}{3} W_{\text{total}}$, it intersects with any prior prepare quorum in at least one honest node, preserving the committed value.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Liveness (Termination)}
\label{sec:liveness_theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Liveness]
\label{thm:liveness}
If the scheduler set $S$ has an honest majority ($\geq \lceil 2m/3 \rceil + 1$ honest schedulers for $m=4$), after GST all message delays are bounded by $\Delta_{\max}$, and $f_j < k_j/3$, then all honest nodes in $C(\tau_j)$ eventually commit a decision for task $\tau_j$ within $T_{\max}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof Sketch]
Under partial synchrony, after GST all messages are delivered within $\Delta_{\max}$.

\textbf{Stage 1: Scheduler consensus.} With $m=4$, $f_s=1$, scheduler PBFT completes within $6\Delta_{\max}$ after GST.

\textbf{Stage 2: Domain broadcast.} Schedulers broadcast $C(\tau_j)$; all honest agents receive it within $\Delta_{\max}$.

\textbf{Stage 3: Normal-path agent consensus.} If the coordinator is honest, the three-phase protocol completes within $6\Delta_{\max}$ (2 message rounds $\times$ $3\Delta_{\max}$).

\textbf{Stage 4: View-change (if coordinator fails).} Honest nodes' timers expire after $\tau_{\text{to}} = 3\Delta_{\max}$. Each view-change attempt completes within $3\Delta_{\max}$ after GST. After at most $f+1$ view changes, an honest coordinator is elected. View-change overhead:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
T_{\text{vc}} \leq (f+1) \cdot 3\Delta_{\max}
\label{eq:vc_latency}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

\textbf{Total latency bound:}
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
T_{\max} &= \underbrace{6\Delta_{\max}}_{\text{scheduler PBFT}}
          + \underbrace{\Delta_{\max}}_{\text{broadcast}}
          + \underbrace{6\Delta_{\max}}_{\text{agent consensus}}
          + \underbrace{(f+1) \cdot 3\Delta_{\max}}_{\text{view-change}} \\
         &= (13 + 3f) \cdot \Delta_{\max}
\label{eq:tmax}
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For $f < k/3$ with typical $k \leq 10$ (i.e., $f \leq 3$): $T_{\max} \leq 22\Delta_{\max}$. For the common case of no view-change ($f_{\text{active}} = 0$): $T_{\max} = 13\Delta_{\max}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The value $T_{\max} = 9\Delta_{\max}$ cited in Section~\ref{sec:agent_com_model} corresponds to the \emph{agent consensus only} (no view-change, no scheduler overhead): $6\Delta_{\max}$ for three-phase protocol plus $3\Delta_{\max}$ for the pre-prepare broadcast. The full end-to-end bound including scheduler PBFT and worst-case view-change is $(13 + 3f)\Delta_{\max}$ as derived above.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{Communication Complexity}
\label{sec:complexity_theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Communication Complexity]
\label{thm:complexity}
For task $\tau_j$ with $k$ nodes and $m=4$ scheduler replicas, STLC achieves $O(m^2 + mk + k^2)$ message complexity per consensus round (normal path), compared to $O(N^2)$ for global PBFT. Under view-change, each view adds $O(k^2)$ messages; with at most $f+1$ view changes, worst-case complexity is $O((f+1) \cdot k^2 + m^2 + mk)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Normal path: Scheduler consensus $O(m^2) = 16$, domain broadcast $O(mk) = 12$, agent consensus $O(k^2) = 9$ (for $k=3$, $m=4$). Total: $O(m^2 + mk + k^2) = O(k^2)$ for constant $m$. View-change: Each round requires $O(k)$ VIEW-CHANGE messages and $O(k)$ NEW-VIEW messages, plus $O(k^2)$ for restarted consensus. With at most $f+1$ view changes: $O((f+1) \cdot k^2)$ additional messages. For $k=3$, $m=4$, $f=1$, $N=100$: STLC uses at most $37 + 2 \times 9 = 55$ messages vs.\ PBFT's 19,900 (99.7\% reduction).
\end{proof}

Table~\ref{tab:pbft_comparison} summarizes STLC's advantages over traditional PBFT.
