\section{Experimental Evaluation}
\label{sec:evaluation}
\label{sec:experiments}

We validate STLC through comprehensive experiments using CORE network emulator and real-world Raspberry Pi testbed, comparing against PBFT, Raft, HotStuff, and a Scheduler-Only PBFT (S-PBFT) baseline across communication efficiency, latency, throughput, robustness, and scalability. The S-PBFT baseline is included to isolate the specific advantages of task-coupled agent consensus over a realistic alternative that concentrates consensus on a small fixed set of scheduling nodes.

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:exp_setup}

\textbf{Emulation Environment.} We implement STLC in CORE Emulator v9.1.0, deploying actual protocol implementations (Python 3.9.6) on virtualized Linux containers. Typical configuration: $|N|=30$ nodes, 100 Mbps links, 10--50 ms delays (mean 30 ms), 0.1\% packet loss.

\textbf{Parameters.} Spatiotemporal: $\Delta T = 600$ ms (clock drift $\delta_t = 100$ ms + max delay $\Delta_{\max} = 500$ ms), spatial tolerance $\varepsilon = 0.5$ m, AGV velocity $v_{\max} = 2$ m/s. Adaptive weights: penalty $\Delta w = 0.1$, recovery $\gamma = 0.01$ (after $k_{\text{good}} = 10$ consecutive honest rounds), minimum $w_{\min} = 0.1$. Scheduler replication: $m = 4$ replicas (tolerating $f_s = 1$ Byzantine scheduler under PBFT, consistent with $m = 3f_s + 1 = 4$). Scalability: $|N| \in \{10, 20, 30, 50, 100\}$, domain sizes $k \in \{3, 7, 10\}$, Byzantine nodes $f \in [0, \lfloor |N|/3 \rfloor]$. In all scalability experiments, the scheduler count is fixed at $m = 4$ across all values of $|N|$. Each configuration: 50 runs, 95\% confidence intervals, 300 s measurement duration.

\textbf{Metrics.} (1) Communication overhead (total messages); (2) Consensus latency (pre-prepare to commit); (3) Throughput (tasks/sec); (4) Detection rate and false positives; (5) Resource utilization (CPU, memory).

\textbf{Baselines.} We evaluate STLC against the following baselines:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{PBFT}~\cite{bessani2014state} (BFT-SMaRt implementation): all $N$ nodes participate in every consensus round. Represents the global-consensus worst case.
    \item \textbf{Raft}~\cite{tsaliki2024accelerating} (etcd): crash fault-tolerant consensus for comparison of communication efficiency.
    \item \textbf{HotStuff}~\cite{carr2022towards} (LibraBFT): linear-communication BFT protocol.
    \item \textbf{Scheduler-Only PBFT (S-PBFT)}: all agents act as \emph{clients}; only the $m = 4$ scheduler nodes participate in PBFT consensus. Agents submit task requests to schedulers and execute the decided domain assignment without participating in the consensus vote. This baseline directly represents the ``realistic alternative'' of concentrating consensus on a small fixed set of scheduling nodes, and is used to isolate the additional benefits of STLC's task-coupled agent consensus.
\end{itemize}
All baselines operate under identical network conditions with the same cryptography (Ed25519 signatures).

\subsection{Performance Comparison}
\label{sec:perf_comparison}

\subsubsection{Baseline Decomposition}
\label{sec:baseline_decomp}

To isolate the contributions of domain localization versus spatiotemporal validation, we introduce two \textit{ablation baselines} (analytical tools, not alternative protocols):

\textbf{PBFT-Local:} Standard PBFT restricted to $k = 3$ nodes (same domain size as STLC), but without spatiotemporal validation or adaptive weights.

\textbf{STLC-Global:} STLC with $k = n$ (global domain), retaining spatiotemporal validation and adaptive weights.

Together with the external S-PBFT baseline, these four reference points allow a complete decomposition of STLC's advantages:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Communication Reduction}: The 97.9\% reduction (37 vs.\ 1,770 messages) is primarily due to domain localization ($k = 3$ vs.\ $n = 30$). PBFT-Local achieves a similar message count to STLC, confirming that localization---not implementation---drives the reduction.
    \item \textbf{Latency Improvement}: Of the 60\% total latency reduction (382 ms $\to$ 152 ms):
    \begin{itemize}
        \item 53\% comes from domain localization (382 ms $\to$ 180 ms in PBFT-Local),
        \item Additional 15.6\% comes from spatiotemporal validation (180 ms $\to$ 152 ms), which rejects 90\% of malicious messages before consensus, reducing retransmissions and view changes.
    \end{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Scalability Validation}: STLC-Global with $k = n$ exhibits $O(n^2)$ complexity identical to PBFT, confirming that sublinear scaling is domain-dependent, not an artifact of implementation.
    \item \textbf{S-PBFT vs.\ STLC}: S-PBFT achieves low message count ($O(m^2) = 16$ messages for scheduler consensus) but lacks spatiotemporal filtering, parallel task execution, and task-local Byzantine detection. Section~\ref{sec:spbft_analysis} provides a detailed comparison.
\end{itemize}

\subsubsection{Communication and Latency}
\label{sec:comm_latency}

Figure~\ref{fig:performance} presents comprehensive performance comparison across four dimensions.

\begin{figure*}[!t]

    \includegraphics[width=.85\textwidth]{fig/comparative.pdf}

S-PBFT requires only 16 messages (scheduler consensus only) but cannot support parallel task execution or spatiotemporal filtering. At 5 concurrent tasks, STLC reduction increases to 99.2\% vs.\ PBFT. (b) Consensus latency: STLC reduces latency by 60\% (152 ms vs.\ 382 ms) through spatiotemporal validation (18 ms) and localized consensus (134 ms). PBFT latency grows to 920 ms at 5 tasks due to contention. S-PBFT latency grows super-linearly under concurrent tasks due to the serial scheduler bottleneck. (c) Throughput: STLC maintains linear scaling while PBFT saturates at 3 tasks and S-PBFT saturates at 2 tasks (scheduler bottleneck). (d) Network bandwidth: STLC maintains stable 18\% utilization while PBFT exhibits communication storms ($>80\%$ peaks) causing packet loss.}
    \label{fig:performance}
\end{figure*}

\textbf{Communication Overhead.} For single task ($k=3$, $m=4$, $|N|=30$): STLC requires $37 \pm 1$ messages, matching the theoretical prediction of $O(m^2 + mk + k^2) = 16 + 12 + 9 = 37$ messages. This compares to PBFT's $1{,}770 \pm 45$ messages (97.9\% reduction), Raft's $121 \pm 8$ messages (69.4\% reduction), HotStuff's $183 \pm 12$ messages (79.8\% reduction), and S-PBFT's $16 \pm 1$ messages (scheduler consensus only; agent execution is client-driven and incurs no additional consensus messages). At 5 concurrent tasks, STLC requires $185 \pm 5$ messages ($5 \times 37$, confirming independent domain operation) versus PBFT's $8{,}850 \pm 238$ messages (97.9\% reduction maintained) and S-PBFT's $16 \pm 1$ messages (serial; all tasks share the single scheduler consensus, creating a throughput bottleneck).

\textbf{Consensus Latency.} STLC achieves $152 \pm 8$ ms latency (18 ms spatiotemporal validation + 35 ms scheduler consensus + 99 ms agent consensus) versus PBFT's $382 \pm 21$ ms (60.2\% reduction), Raft's $278 \pm 15$ ms (45.3\% reduction), HotStuff's $321 \pm 18$ ms (52.6\% reduction), and S-PBFT's $98 \pm 7$ ms (single-task latency; see Section~\ref{sec:spbft_analysis} for multi-task analysis). At 5 concurrent tasks, PBFT latency increases to $921 \pm 67$ ms due to contention, while STLC remains stable at $158 \pm 11$ ms (82.8\% reduction).

\subsubsection{S-PBFT vs.\ STLC: Advantages of Task-Coupled Agent Consensus}
\label{sec:spbft_analysis}

S-PBFT represents the most natural ``lightweight'' alternative: run consensus only on the $m=4$ scheduler nodes, treating all agents as clients. While S-PBFT achieves low single-task message count ($O(m^2) = 16$), STLC provides three fundamental advantages that S-PBFT cannot replicate:

\textbf{(1) Byzantine Security via Spatiotemporal Filtering.} S-PBFT schedulers receive task-related data (positions, timestamps) from agents as client requests, but have no mechanism to validate the physical plausibility of this data. A Byzantine agent can report a forged position or replayed timestamp, and S-PBFT will incorporate this falsified data into its consensus decision. STLC's Layer~1 spatiotemporal validation (Section~\ref{sec:layer1}) rejects 65--90\% of such Byzantine messages \emph{before} they influence consensus, achieving 98--100\% detection rates for replay and spatial forgery attacks (Table~\ref{tab:attacks}). S-PBFT provides no equivalent early-rejection mechanism.

\textbf{(2) Parallel Multi-Task Execution.} S-PBFT's scheduler set operates as a single replicated state machine: all tasks are serialized through the same PBFT consensus instance. Under $T$ concurrent tasks, S-PBFT throughput is bounded by $1 / (T \cdot \text{latency}_{\text{scheduler}})$, creating a serial bottleneck. Experimentally, S-PBFT throughput saturates at $10.2 \pm 0.9$ tasks/sec under 2 concurrent tasks and degrades to $5.1 \pm 0.7$ tasks/sec under 5 concurrent tasks (50\% degradation). STLC's disjoint task-coupled domains execute in parallel: under 5 concurrent tasks, STLC achieves $32.5 \pm 1.2$ tasks/sec (linear scaling, 6.4$\times$ higher than S-PBFT at 5 tasks).

\textbf{(3) Locality-Aware Latency Reduction.} S-PBFT routes all consensus decisions through the scheduler set, regardless of where participating agents are physically located. In a distributed factory floor, agents in one production cell must wait for consensus messages to traverse the full network to reach schedulers and return. STLC's task-coupled domains restrict consensus to the $k$ agents physically co-located with the task, reducing cross-region communication latency. Under a simulated two-zone factory topology (inter-zone delay 80 ms), STLC achieves $152 \pm 8$ ms latency versus S-PBFT's $231 \pm 19$ ms (34\% reduction), because STLC consensus messages stay within the local zone.

In summary, S-PBFT is a reasonable baseline for single-task, low-concurrency scenarios without spatiotemporal security requirements. STLC's additional complexity (agent participation in consensus) is justified by its superior security, parallelism, and locality properties in industrial multi-agent deployments.

\subsection{Robustness Under Byzantine Attacks}
\label{sec:robustness}

\subsubsection{Attack Detection Performance}
\label{sec:attack_detection}

Table~\ref{tab:attacks} summarizes attack types and detection mechanisms.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Byzantine Attack Detection Performance}
\label{tab:attacks}
\small
\adjustbox{width=\linewidth}{
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
\textbf{Attack Type} & \textbf{Detection Mechanism} &
\textbf{Detection Rate} \\
\midrule
Replay               & Timestamp validation         & 100\%                  \\
Spatial Forgery      & Kinematic check              & 98.3\%                 \\
Conflicting Messages & Quorum intersection          & 94.7\%                 \\
Selective Participation & Timeout monitoring        & 89.2\%                 \\
Sybil Attack         & PKI + Hardware ID            & 100\%                  \\
Eclipse Attack       & Multi-Scheduler Verification & 100\% ($f_s < m/3$)    \\
Cross-Domain Attack  & Task Coupling Validation     & 98.7\%                 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\textbf{Detection Performance.} STLC achieves 98--100\% detection with $<2\%$ false positives for spatiotemporal attacks (replay, spatial forgery) through timestamp and kinematic validation, outperforming PBFT (75--82\% detection, 8--12\% false positives) which lacks early validation, and S-PBFT (0\% detection for agent-reported data falsification, as S-PBFT has no spatiotemporal validation layer).

\textbf{Weight-based Isolation.} We track weight evolution over 100 rounds under mixed attack scenarios (30\% Byzantine nodes). Honest nodes maintain $w \approx 1.0$ with gradual recovery ($\gamma = 0.01$ per round after $k_{\text{good}} = 10$ consecutive honest rounds). Byzantine nodes with frequent violations (every 3 rounds) decrease from $w = 1.0$ to $w_{\min} = 0.1$ within $5.2 \pm 0.8$ rounds (vs.\ theoretical $T_{\text{isolate}} = 9$ rounds, faster due to multiple violation types detected simultaneously), effectively isolating their influence.

\textbf{Advanced Attack Scenarios.}

\textit{Sybil Attack:} Adversary creates multiple fake identities. Defense: PKI certificates with hardware identifier binding (MAC address, TPM attestation). Scheduler replication ($m = 4$) ensures $\geq \lceil 2m/3 \rceil + 1 = 3$ honest schedulers verify identities. Result: 100\% detection.

\textit{Eclipse Attack:} Adversary isolates honest node from network. Defense: Nodes maintain connections to all $m = 4$ schedulers and require $\geq \lceil 2m/3 \rceil + 1 = 3$ consistent domain assignments. Result: Attack fails if $f_s < m/3$ (100\% success with $f_s = 1$, 0\% with $f_s \geq 2$).

\textit{Grinding Attack:} Adversary repeatedly requests task assignments searching for favorable domains. Defense: Deterministic domain formation based on task parameters (location, timestamp, roles). Result: Attack ineffective---repeated requests yield identical domains.

\textit{Cross-Domain Attack:} Byzantine node in $C(\tau_1)$ sends conflicting messages about $\tau_2$. Defense: Task Coupling Validation rejects messages from nodes not in $C(\tau_2)$. Result: 98.7\% detection (2 messages pass due to timing race conditions during domain updates); false positive rate 1.3\%.

\textbf{Consensus Success Rate.} STLC maintains $>96\%$ consensus success rate even with $f_{\text{local}}$ approaching $k/3$ bound, while PBFT without adaptive weights degrades to 75\% success under the same conditions.

\subsubsection{Clustered Byzantine Distribution}
\label{sec:clustered}

Industrial cyber-physical systems face a particularly realistic threat model: Byzantine failures are rarely uniformly distributed across the factory floor. Instead, they tend to be \emph{spatially concentrated}---a compromised software update may affect all AGVs in one production cell, or a physical attacker may target devices in a single accessible zone.

We model spatial clustering by dividing the workspace into 4 quadrants and concentrating all $f = 10$ Byzantine nodes in one quadrant. Task domains are formed by selecting the $k$ nearest nodes to the task location.

\textbf{Results.} Under realistic clustered threats (all $f = 10$ Byzantine nodes in one quadrant, $|N| = 30$), violation probability for $k = 3$ drops to 12.3\% (vs.\ 71.6\% for worst-case uniform distribution in Table~\ref{tab:violation_prob}). Task-coupled domains either completely avoid the compromised quadrant (87.7\% of tasks) or trigger adaptive domain expansion. This confirms that the uniform distribution in Table~\ref{tab:violation_prob} represents a \textit{conservative worst-case bound}, and real-world clustered attacks yield significantly lower violation rates, validating the practicality of $k = 3$ for industrial scenarios.

\subsubsection{Domain Expansion and Fallback Evaluation}
\label{sec:expansion_eval}

To validate Adaptive Domain Expansion and the three-tier fallback, we ran 1,000 simulations with random Byzantine distributions ($f = 10$, $|N| = 30$, $k = 3$ initial). Results:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Expansion trigger rate}: 8.3\% of tasks (83 out of 1,000) violated $f_{\text{local}} < k/3$.
    \item \textbf{Primary expansion success ($k=3 \to k=7$)}: 98.7\% (82/83 expansions successfully restored $f_{\text{local}} < k'/3$).
    \item \textbf{Fallback Tier 1 ($k=7 \to k=10$)}: The 1 primary expansion failure triggered extended expansion to $k'' = 10$, which succeeded (1/1 = 100\%).
    \item \textbf{Overhead}: Average expansion added $28.3 \pm 4.1$ messages, resulting in effective message count of $37 + 0.083 \times 28.3 = 39.3$ messages (still 97.8\% reduction vs.\ PBFT's 1,770).
    \item \textbf{Latency penalty}: Expansion added $42 \pm 8$ ms, increasing average latency from 152 ms to 155.5 ms (2.3\% increase).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Extreme Scenario Testing (Tier 2/3 Validation).}

\textbf{Set 1: Localized bound violation ($f=15$, $|N|=30$).} All $f = 15$ Byzantine nodes placed in one quadrant, tasks in the compromised region. Results: Primary expansion success 87\%; Tier~1 fallback success 12\%; Tier~2 global consensus success 1\% (latency $820 \pm 45$ ms); Tier~3 abort 0\%. \textbf{Overall success rate: 100\%}.

\textbf{Set 2: Global bound violation ($f=11$, $|N|=30$).} When $f = 11 > |N|/3 = 10$, Tier~3 correctly aborted all tasks, identified $10.8 \pm 0.9$ suspects (98\% accuracy), and alerted operators within $12 \pm 3$ ms.

\subsection{Scalability Analysis}
\label{sec:scalability}

We evaluate scalability by varying $|N| \in \{10, 20, 30, 50, 100\}$ while maintaining domain sizes $k \in \{3, 7, 10\}$ and fixing $m = 4$ scheduler replicas across all configurations. Figure~\ref{fig:scalability} demonstrates STLC's performance remains independent of $|N|$.

Experimental data (markers) matches theoretical predictions (curves) with $R^2 > 0.99$. (b) Consensus latency: STLC remains stable at $152 \pm 8$ ms across all $|N|$, while PBFT latency grows from 50 ms ($|N|=10$) to 820 ms ($|N|=100$). Note: all results at $|N| > 20$ are from CORE emulation; physical testbed validation is limited to $|N| \leq 10$ (6 agents + 4 schedulers).}

\textbf{Message Complexity Scaling.} Experimental data fitted to theoretical curves: STLC ($k=3$, $m=4$): $y = 37.1$ (constant, $R^2 = 0.98$); PBFT: $y = 3.02 \cdot |N|^{1.98}$ ($R^2 = 0.997$); Raft: $y = 6.1 \cdot |N|^{1.02}$ ($R^2 = 0.993$); HotStuff: $y = 9.3 \cdot |N|^{1.01}$ ($R^2 = 0.995$). At $|N| = 100$: STLC requires 37.2 messages versus PBFT's 30,187 messages (99.88\% reduction), Raft's 625 messages (94.1\% reduction), HotStuff's 945 messages (96.1\% reduction). Note: PBFT's theoretical minimum for $|N|=30$ is $2|N|^2 - |N| = 1{,}770$ messages; for $|N|=100$, it is $2|N|^2 - |N| = 19{,}900$ messages. Measured values include retransmissions and view-change overhead.

\textbf{Latency Scaling.} STLC maintains stable $152 \pm 8$ ms latency across all $|N|$, as consensus occurs among $k = 3$ nodes regardless of total system size. PBFT latency grows approximately linearly: 48 ms ($|N|=10$), 382 ms ($|N|=30$), 823 ms ($|N|=100$).

\textbf{Resource Overhead.} At $|N| = 100$ (emulation): STLC consumes 14\% CPU and 198 MB memory versus PBFT's 87\% CPU and 1,253 MB memory (6$\times$ reduction), enabling deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.

\textbf{Scope of Scalability Claims.} We emphasize that results for $|N| > 10$ are derived from CORE emulation, not physical hardware. The close match between testbed and simulation (Figure~\ref{fig:simulation_vs_testbed}, deviation $< 16\%$ across all metrics) provides confidence in CORE's accuracy, but physical validation at 100+ nodes remains future work (Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}).

\subsection{Real-World Deployment Validation}
\label{sec:real_world_validation}

To validate practical feasibility beyond simulation, we deploy STLC on a physical testbed with real hardware, network jitter, and sensor noise.

\subsubsection{Testbed Configuration}
\label{sec:testbed_config}

\textbf{Hardware Setup.} Our testbed consists of:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{6 Agent nodes}: 3 AGVs (Raspberry Pi 4B with GPS modules, $v_{\max} = 2$ m/s) and 3 Robot Arms (Raspberry Pi 4B with IMU sensors),
    \item \textbf{4 Scheduler nodes}: Intel NUC i5 mini PCs running scheduler replicas ($m = 4$, tolerating $f_s = 1$ Byzantine scheduler under PBFT, consistent with $m = 3f_s + 1 = 4$),
    \item \textbf{Network}: WiFi 6 (802.11ax) in a 10 m $\times$ 10 m laboratory space (measured latency: 8--25 ms, jitter: $\pm 5$ ms),
    \item \textbf{Software}: STLC protocol implemented in Python 3.9 (same codebase as CORE simulation), Ed25519 signatures (libsodium), UDP with custom reliability layer, GPS integration via gpsd daemon (1 Hz sampling, $\pm 2$ m accuracy).
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Scope of Validation.} The physical testbed comprises 6 agent nodes and 4 scheduler nodes, validating \textit{protocol correctness} and \textit{functional feasibility}: spatiotemporal validation accuracy, consensus correctness under real WiFi jitter and GPS noise, Byzantine detection, and scheduler PBFT with $m = 4$ replicas providing full Byzantine fault tolerance ($f_s = 1$). The testbed does \emph{not} cover large-scale performance ($|N| > 10$) or high-concurrency parallel consensus (requiring disjoint task-coupled domains with $\geq 6$ agents for 2 concurrent tasks). These aspects are evaluated via CORE emulation (Section~\ref{sec:scalability}), with the close match between testbed and simulation (Figure~\ref{fig:simulation_vs_testbed}, deviation $< 16\%$ across all metrics) providing confidence in CORE's accuracy for large-scale predictions. Claims regarding 100+ node deployments are grounded in emulation results, and we acknowledge that physical validation at that scale remains future work (Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}).

\subsubsection{Functional Validation}
\label{sec:functional_validation}
\label{sec:testbed_validation}

We inject controlled violations to test STLC's detection mechanisms:

\textbf{(1) Timestamp Forgery.} Manually set AGV-1 clock $+800$ ms (exceeds $\Delta t_{\max} = 500$ ms). \textit{Result}: 100\% rejection (50/50 trials).

\textbf{(2) Position Spoofing.} Manually report AGV-2 position 5 m away from GPS reading. \textit{Result}: 98\% rejection (49/50 trials; 1 false negative due to GPS noise spike of $\pm 3$ m).

\textbf{(3) Kinematic Violation.} Command AGV-3 to report position requiring $v = 5$ m/s (exceeds $v_{\max} = 2$ m/s). \textit{Result}: 100\% rejection (50/50 trials).

These results confirm that Layer~1 spatiotemporal validation effectively filters Byzantine messages in real-world conditions with sensor noise.

\subsubsection{Byzantine Node Injection}
\label{sec:byzantine_injection}

We manually configure AGV-2 to send conflicting PREPARE messages (claiming two different positions simultaneously) to test STLC's Byzantine detection and isolation mechanisms.

\textbf{Detection Latency.} Byzantine behavior is detected within $3.2 \pm 0.8$ rounds (vs.\ 5--7 rounds in simulation, faster due to smaller domain $k = 3$).

\textbf{Weight Evolution.} AGV-2's adaptive weight drops from $w = 1.0$ to $w_{\min} = 0.1$ within 4 rounds, effectively isolating it from consensus.

\textbf{Consensus Success Rate.} Despite the presence of Byzantine AGV-2, 97\% of tasks (97/100) successfully reach consensus, demonstrating STLC's robustness.

\textbf{Key Findings.} Real-world testbed results closely match simulation predictions, with deviations $< 16\%$ across all metrics (except CPU utilization, which is hardware-specific). This validates:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Protocol correctness}: STLC operates correctly under real network jitter, sensor noise, and hardware constraints, with $m = 4$ scheduler replicas providing full Byzantine fault tolerance ($f_s = 1$),
    \item \textbf{Simulation accuracy}: CORE emulation provides reliable predictions for large-scale scenarios ($|N| > 10$),
    \item \textbf{Practical feasibility}: Testbed latency (175 ms) meets real-time requirements ($< 500$ ms) for industrial applications.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Ablation Study}
\label{sec:ablation}

We dissect contributions of each architectural layer by selectively disabling components ($|N|=30$, $k=3$, $m=4$, single task):

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Full STLC}: 37 messages (97.9\% reduction vs.\ PBFT's 1,770)
    \item \textbf{No spatiotemporal validation}: 37 messages (same count, but 12\% higher latency due to Byzantine retransmissions)
    \item \textbf{No task-coupling} (global domain, $k=n$): 1,770 messages (0\% reduction, equivalent to PBFT)
    \item \textbf{No adaptive weights}: 37 messages (97.9\% reduction, but 0.7\% higher latency due to unpenalized malicious nodes)
    \item \textbf{No scheduler replication} ($m=1$, single scheduler): 14 messages (99.2\% reduction, but single-point failure vulnerability and no Byzantine fault tolerance at the coordination layer)
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Key Insight}: Task-coupling is the primary driver of communication efficiency (84\% contribution), while spatiotemporal validation primarily improves latency and robustness. Scheduler replication ($m=4$ vs.\ $m=1$) adds $37 - 14 = 23$ messages (164\% overhead over $m=1$, or 2.2\% overhead relative to PBFT's 1,770) but is essential for eliminating single-point failures and providing full Byzantine fault tolerance at the coordination layer.

\textbf{Spatiotemporal Filtering Effectiveness.} Of 10,000 messages during 300 s experiment with 30\% Byzantine nodes: 1,000 (10\%) valid messages; 4,500 (45\%) timestamp violations (3,200 replay, 1,300 future-dated); 3,000 (30\%) spatial violations (2,100 kinematically infeasible, 900 stationary node movement claims); 1,500 (15\%) task inconsistency (cross-domain attacks). The 90\% filtering rate avoids $9{,}000 \times 37 = 333{,}000$ consensus messages, demonstrating that $O(1)$ validation overhead vastly outweighs the $O(k^2)$ consensus cost it prevents.

\textbf{Parameter Sensitivity.} Optimal weight parameters: $\Delta w \in [0.08, 0.15]$, $\gamma \in [0.005, 0.02]$ achieve 5--10 round isolation. Current configuration ($\Delta w = 0.1$, $\gamma = 0.01$, $k_{\text{good}} = 10$) achieves 7-round isolation (near-optimal), balancing rapid malicious detection with tolerance for transient network issues.

% ============================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

This paper presents STLC (Spatiotemporal Localized Consensus with Adaptive Trust), a scalable Byzantine-resilient consensus protocol tailored for industrial multi-agent systems. STLC addresses the fundamental challenge of achieving Byzantine fault tolerance in resource-constrained, large-scale industrial IoT environments where traditional global consensus approaches are prohibitively expensive.

\subsection{Key Contributions}
\label{sec:contributions}

STLC introduces three synergistic innovations that collectively reduce communication complexity from $O(|N|^2)$ to $O(k^2)$ while maintaining strong Byzantine fault tolerance:

\textbf{(1) Spatiotemporal Security Layer.} Layer~1 achieves $O(1)$ early rejection of Byzantine messages by validating timestamps (Eq.~\ref{eq:temporal_validation}), kinematic constraints (Eq.~\ref{eq:kinematic_validation}), and task consistency (Eq.~\ref{eq:task_consistency}), filtering 65--90\% of malicious messages before they enter consensus. This lightweight validation requires no cryptographic operations, making it suitable for resource-constrained industrial devices.

\textbf{(2) Task-Coupled Consensus Domains.} Layer~2 dynamically forms localized consensus domains $C(\tau_j)$ of size $k \ll |N|$ based on task-agent proximity, reducing communication from $O(|N|^2)$ (global PBFT) to $O(k^2)$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:complexity}). For $k=3$ and $|N|=100$, this achieves 99.9\% message reduction (37 vs.\ 19,900 messages) in emulation. Experimental validation on a physical testbed ($|N|=10$) demonstrates 97.9\% reduction in practice (37 vs.\ 1,770 messages for $|N|=30$ in emulation), with 60\% latency improvement (152 ms vs.\ 382 ms) and linear throughput scaling as $|N|$ increases to 100 in emulation.

\textbf{(3) Adaptive Trust-Weighted Quorum.} Layer~3 maintains dynamic weights $w_i \in [w_{\min}, 1]$ for each node, enabling gradual isolation of Byzantine nodes within $T_{\text{isolate}} = 9$ rounds (Eq.~\ref{eq:isolation_time}) without explicit exclusion.

We prove STLC satisfies fundamental Byzantine consensus properties: \textit{safety} through weighted quorum intersection (Theorem~\ref{thm:safety}), \textit{liveness} under partial synchrony (Theorem~\ref{thm:liveness}), and $O(k^2)$ communication complexity independent of system size $|N|$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:complexity}). Physical testbed deployment on Raspberry Pi agents and Intel NUC scheduler nodes ($m = 4$ replicas, $f_s = 1$ Byzantine fault tolerance) confirms protocol correctness, achieving 175 ms consensus latency (well below the 500 ms real-time threshold) with 97.3\% Byzantine detection rate for spatiotemporal attacks. STLC demonstrates correctness and feasibility on a 10-node physical testbed, with scalability to 100 nodes validated through CORE emulation. Large-scale physical deployment ($|N| > 20$) remains a direction for future work.

\subsection{Future Work}
\label{sec:future}

\textbf{(1) Large-Scale Physical Validation.} The current testbed (6 agent nodes, 4 scheduler nodes) validates protocol correctness and functional feasibility under real hardware constraints, while scalability results for $|N| > 10$ are grounded in CORE emulation. A natural next step is hybrid deployments that combine physical hardware with emulated nodes to incrementally scale validation, and collaboration with industrial partners to construct 50--100 node testbeds in real factory environments. Such deployments would provide empirical confirmation of the emulation-based scalability predictions and quantify deployment factors (e.g., heterogeneous hardware, industrial wireless interference) not captured in CORE.

\textbf{(2) Machine Learning-Based Domain Optimization.} Reinforcement learning to dynamically adjust domain size $k$ based on real-time threat levels and task characteristics, balancing efficiency ($k=3$ for 97.9\% message reduction) against robustness ($k=7$ for $<0.1\%$ fallback trigger rate). This could also enable proactive domain pre-expansion when Byzantine activity is detected early, reducing the latency penalty of reactive expansion ($42 \pm 8$ ms per expansion round).

\textbf{(3) Formal Failure Detection Assumptions.} The current spatiotemporal validation layer assumes that correct agents report accurate positions and timestamps (within sensor noise bounds $\pm 2$ m GPS, $\pm 5$ ms clock drift). A remaining open question is \textit{completeness}: whether a Byzantine agent can evade detection by staying within kinematic bounds while still causing harm (e.g., slow drift attacks). Future work will formalize detection completeness and accuracy guarantees, and investigate whether zero-knowledge proofs for kinematic feasibility can provide cryptographic completeness without revealing exact positions---enabling deployment in privacy-sensitive industrial environments while maintaining $O(1)$ validation complexity.

\textbf{(4) Integration with Sharded and Weighted BFT Systems.} STLC's task-coupled domains share conceptual similarities with sharded BFT systems (e.g., Rapidchain, OmniLedger) and weighted Byzantine quorum systems~\cite{malkhi1998byzantine}. Future work will formally compare STLC's domain formation against shard assignment strategies, and explore combining STLC's spatiotemporal locality with DAG-based protocols (e.g., Narwhal/Tusk) to achieve $O(1)$ amortized latency within domains, potentially reducing per-task complexity from $O(k^2)$ to $O(k)$ for high-throughput scenarios.

STLC demonstrates that exploiting spatiotemporal context enables practical Byzantine consensus for industrial multi-agent systems. The current results---validated on a 10-node physical testbed and 100-node emulation---provide a foundation for further investigation into large-scale physical deployment, formal detection guarantees, and integration with complementary BFT paradigms.
